We want to rally around him to let him know that we have his back and we're here for him however he needs us. But the way that he's dealt with it has been unbelievable. "
Oliver, 28, did not play in Saturday's game due to a minor injury. He is entering his eighth season with the Bills, who selected him with the ninth overall pick in the 2019 NFL Draft .
author: Bryan DeArdo

title: Michael Penix Jr. has impressed Falcons behind the scenes. Now fully cleared, the real QB battle begins
summary: Sources say Penix's "live arm" is already turning heads as the quarterback competition in Atlanta officially kicks into high gear
full_text:
Even while limited to just 7-on-7 sessions and individual drills in recent months, there were still moments from Michael Penix Jr . in practice when the 2024 top-10 draft pick was able to stand out and impress the new Atlanta Falcons staff thanks to a certain part of his skill set: a left arm that's capable of delivering throws that many other NFL quarterbacks, including the others in Atlanta, aren't capable of making.
"Some of the balls that jump out of his hand," a source said, "and that kind of live arm, it's impressive to see."
That arm is part of the reason that it will now become an interesting next three weeks in Atlanta leading into the Falcons' regular season opener against the Steelers on Sept. 13.
With Penix -- who has been working from a November ACL injury -- being cleared to fully participate in practice starting Monday, the Falcons are of the mindset that their QB competition can now truly begin.
While it's fair to say that free agent signee Tua Tagovailoa remains the favorite to win Atlanta's starting QB job, Penix will now get a chance these next few weeks to try and prove that he's the better option.
"It's just a true evaluation now with both guys being able to be in the huddle, control the line of scrimmage and control the game flow," a source said. "You're able to get a real sense from that aspect now and who's able to bring this offense to life."
Penix made nine starts last season before suffering the ACL injury, which was the fifth season-ending injury he's suffered since the start of his college career, including the third ACL tear.
Among the good from those nine starts was a touchdown-to-interception ratio of nine-to-three, two games with at least 298 passing yards and a three-touchdown performance vs. the Patriots. Among the bad: A 3-5 record for the Falcons in the games Penix played from start to finish, a completion percentage (60.1) that ranked fourth-worst among NFL QBs that made at least eight starts and a QB rating of 88.5 that tied, coincidentally with Tagovailoa, for just 26th-best in the NFL.
However, Penix will now get his chance to fully show what he can do under Atlanta's new staff and new head coach Kevin Stefanski. Although sources have emphasized that Penix has already done a lot during his work in 7-on-7 and individual drills, the team's practice Monday will give this staff their first look at him in an 11-on-11 setting.
The timing is good for the Falcons.
While a source said that Tagovailoa "has grown, especially (transitioning) from what he was asked to do in Miami and what he's asked to do now," there have also been ups and downs for him this offseason. That includes during the Falcons' preseason opener vs. the Broncos when he was 3 of 5 for 22 yards.
As part of Atlanta's plan, Tagovailoa didn't play in Atlanta's second preseason game but is expected to play in the preseason finale against the Dolphins on Friday. It's unclear as of yet whether Penix will play in that game.
Either way, even if it's just during practice, the Falcons' staff will now get a real chance to evaluate and compare both quarterbacks and then make a determination regarding which is the better option to be the team's starting QB.
That important part of this process starts Monday.
author: Matt Zenitz

title: NFL preseason Week 2 winners and losers: Bo Nix shines in return, Deshaun Watson takes shot at Browns fans
summary: Rookie wideout De'Zhaun Stribling continues his historic preseason run for San Francisco, while Geno Smith shines in his return to New York
full_text:
The second week of the NFL preseason is underway, with the regular season drawing ever closer.
Preseason football is like a box of chocolates as Forrest Gump would say, "You never know what you're going to get." That's because some squads have their starters chained to the bench, some play minimal snaps and some could receive as much of a half of work. Observing who could emerge as a real contributor from the chaos that is preseason football is tricky given the varying degrees of skill levels on the field all at the same time, but it's possible to identify who maximized their opportunity and who would like a do-over.
Let's kick identify the winners and losers of Week 2 of the 2026 preseason.
Was Shedeur Sanders perfect in his preseason Week 2 start? Hardly. Was he much, much better than Deshaun Watson ? Absolutely. (Though the bar was basically on the ground).
Sanders came out firing after having to wait out a weather delay of nearly an hour, connecting on all four of his passes on the opening drive. That included a fourth-down conversion to tight end Blake Whiteheart and, later on, an 8-yard touchdown pass to Luke Floriea . Sanders had a few of Cleveland's starters -- namely rookies Spencer Fano and Denzel Boston -- out there with him, but he was mostly working with backups. The Bills rested basically all of their starters, too.
the second year connection for the TD! #BUFvsCLE on News 5 pic.twitter.com/BntGdJpIAM
"There's a lot there to like," coach Todd Monken said. "I mean he plays with a certain amount of confidence. He has gotten a lot better at getting rid of the ball. Certainly he wants to make a play.
"... I thought he did a lot of really good things. I'm really proud of him and where he's come from. From the moment I got here until now, very impressive."
Monken in specific cited the above touchdown pass and a 23-yard completion on third and 15 as two of Sanders' best moments.
Sanders actually hit on his first eight passes in a row before an interception in which he threw slightly behind Jermaine Terry II . Monken said the ball "certainly" could have been caught. It also could have been a better throw.
Damar Hamlin comes up with the INT 🙌 BUFvsCLE on @nflnetwork Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/SBow1PXq6x
Overall, it was a strong day for Sanders -- 9-for-11, 74 yards, one touchdown, one interception, one sack -- and a much better outing than in Week 1.
Preseason scores do not matter at all, but there might not have been a single team needing a good week more than the Falcons . Atlanta got walloped by Denver, 27-7, last week, hours after the news came out that James Pearce Jr . was suspended eight games . Tua Tagovailoa looked awful, the defense looked awful, and the vibes were bad.
Week 2 was much better. With no Tagovailoa or Michael Penix Jr . playing, Cooper Rush and Jack Strand both played well, and three different players had a rushing touchdown in a 34-6 win over the Colts .
The best news, however, came after the game: Kevin Stefanski said Penix has been cleared to return to 11-on-11 work after a lengthy rehabilitation from yet another torn ACL. Maybe Tagovailoa is already the de-facto starter since it's taken Penix a bit, but it's always nice to get positive injury updates.
San Francisco 49ers 2026 second-round pick wide receiver De'Zhaun Stribling , the rookie 33rd overall pick out of Ole Miss, is THE breakout star of the preseason this year. After catching four of his five targets for 46 yards receiving on Thursday against the Los Angeles Chargers , Stribling is now up to 11 catches for 109 yards receiving on 13 targets. That makes Stribling the first player since at least 2017 to produce at least 11 catches combined within the first 20 minutes of two consecutive preseason games, per CBS Sports Research. Many preseason All-Stars don't end up contributing much outside of special teams for their respective squads, but it's safe to say Stribling will have a place on head coach Kyle Shanahan's play call sheet early this regular season. That's especially true when factoring in how snake-bitten by injury San Francisco is at the position.
Every De'Zhaun Stribling target from week 2 of the preseason. pic.twitter.com/aDUNARC2WT
No, Will Anderson Jr. , Danielle Hunter , Derek Stingley Jr . and the rest of the starters from the NFL's No. 1 total defense (277.2 total yards per game allowed) in 2025 weren't on the field Thursday night, but the Houston Texans ' ferocious tenacity on defense certainly was.
They bullied Las Vegas Raiders first overall pick rookie quarterback Fernando Mendoza in the first half, generating an 80-yard pick six by fourth-round rookie linebacker Wade Woodaz and an 11-yard sack by second-round rookie defensive tackle Kayden McDonald .
OPEN UP A CAN OF WOODAZZZZZZ 🤯 📺: @nflonespn pic.twitter.com/Ke0lrYupPs
Seeing McDonald flash pass rush chops like this should send shivers down the spines of offensive coordinators all around the league. If there was an area Houston needed to shore up on their defense, it was defensive tackle, and they were able to do so by drafting McDonald, the 2026 NFL Draft's top defensive tackle prospect in the eyes of many, including yours truly. McDonald, who is listed at 6-foot-3-inches tall while weighing 326 pounds, was more of a run stuffer than a pass rusher in college at Ohio State, but if he can find his groove early on when tasked to get after the quarterback, Houston's defense could be a much greater problem for the rest of the league.
KMAC WITH THE SACK 😮‍💨 📺: @nflonespn pic.twitter.com/kOks1uMcrW
Tennessee All-SEC cornerback Jermod McCoy profiled as a likely first-round pick in the 2026 NFL Draft until the medicals surrounding his knee scared teams away. McCoy did suffer a torn ACL in January 2025, but fears about inflammation and arthritis in his knee caused him to tumble all the way down to being the 101st overall pick and a fourth-round draft choice.
In the Raiders' 22-20 preseason victory over the Texans on Thursday, McCoy appeared to be moving well and in phase with opposing wide receivers when tasked with dropping back into man coverage. Perhaps he can end up becoming the best value pick of the 2026 rookie draft class if given the opportunity to receive snaps with Las Vegas' starting defense.
Jermod McCoy man coverage snaps. Talent is there. Very fluid and easy COD. Needs to finish at the catch point. Taunting that gives offense a first after forced incompletion is the opposite of finishing. Need to see him against starters. pic.twitter.com/DFBlIRfOfH
Outside of Minnesota Vikings quarterback J.J. McCarthy , perhaps no other quarterback had a more depressing 2025 season than Geno Smith . The two-time Pro Bowler led the NFL in both sacks taken (55) and interceptions thrown (17) last season while attempting to pilot then-offensive coordinator Chip Kelly's scheme with the Las Vegas Raiders. Those statistics made Smith just the sixth quarterback since the 1970 AFL/NFL merger to lead the NFL in both sacks and interceptions in the same season. Kelly had to trudge back down to the college ranks, where he is now Northwestern's offensive coordinator.
Smith, a second-round pick of the New York Jets in the 2013 NFL Draft, returned to New York after the Jets acquired him and a 2026 seventh-round pick from the Raiders in exchange for a 2026 sixth-round pick. He kicked off his second stint with the Jets with a perfect drive while leading the Jets' starting lineup on the opening possession against the Pittsburgh Steelers on Friday before head coach Aaron Glenn decided he'd seen enough from the 35-year-old veteran quarterback to end his night.
Smith completed all seven of his throws on New York's opening drive, including the 13-yard scoring strike to tight end Jelani Woods . He also connected with both of the Jets' top wide receivers, Garrett Wilson (one catch on one target for 10 yards) and Adonai Mitchell (two catches on two targets for 29 yards), to finish the night with 65 yards passing.…

title: Falcons news: Michael Penix cleared to play; what does it mean for Atlanta?
summary: It’s a lot more fun to put Monday’s Falcons Opening Drive together after the Falcons absolutely dominated the Colts in preseason action on Saturday afternoon. Below, I’ve got some thoughts on Michael Penix Jr. being medically cleared and what it means for this quarterback depth chart. We’ve also got some fun looks back at Saturday’s […]
full_text: Jun 16, 2026; Atlanta, GA, USA; Atlanta Falcons quarterback Michael Penix Jr. (9) reacts while being interviewed by the media during Minicamp. Mandatory Credit: Dale Zanine-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect It’s a lot more fun to put Monday’s Falcons Opening Drive together after the Falcons absolutely dominated the Colts in preseason action on Saturday afternoon. Below, I’ve got some thoughts on Michael Penix Jr. being medically cleared and what it means for this quarterback depth chart . We’ve also got some fun looks back at Saturday’s win over the Colts and the state of the roster , a fantastic article on reasons Falcons fans should be excited about this season despite the quarterback depth chart situation , and don’t miss The Falcoholic’s Question of the Day : Should Jack Strand be this team’s QB3? Falcons Opening Drive: What does a healthy Michael Penix Jr. mean for Atlanta? Every single day Kevin Stefanski takes the podium to speak to the media, somebody asks about the timetable for Michael Penix Jr. to be medically cleared. Now we have the answer to that question. But what we don’t know is whether his change in status means there’s a possibility for Penix to start Week 1. During joint practices with the Colts, Penix participated in 1-on-1s and 7-on-7s, and he mentioned to the media after Thursday’s practice that while he feels healthy, his doctor — and Penix — also had to think about the possibility that he’s not healthy enough to withstand full contact. “If I had a rush coming at me and everything, I could get away, but it’s just right now, if I don’t get away, that’s what we think about,” Penix said during joint practices against the Colts last week. Penix has also spoken several times this offseason and preseason about the mental hurdle associated with his recovery. He’s cleared to participate physically, but has he been able to fully overcome that mental hurdle? And if not, does that create additional injury risk? Is it worth taking the chance? Is his head in the right place? And then there’s the matter of Penix’s injury history, and the injury history of the other potential QB1 on the roster, Tua Tagovailoa . Monday kicks off a fundamentally important week of practice for all four quarterbacks on the roster. Tua Tagovailoa will want to prove he should be the starter regardless of Michael Penix Jr’s status. Penix will want to prove the mental reps he’s taken in addition to his limited physical participation in practice have actually prepared him to start Week 1. For Cooper Rush and Jack Strand , they’re each hoping to snag that QB3 spot. Yes, Tagovailoa and Penix are both healthy now, but because of their injury histories, making sure the QB3 is adequate is fundamentally important. I can understand the thought process behind keeping Rush and his experience around, but Strand has truly been exciting to watch this preseason, and his potential is massive. Kevin Stefanski will speak to the media around noon tomorrow, practice will be at 2:35 p.m., and select players (I won’t know who until tomorrow) will speak to the media after practice. I typically can’t be in Flowery Branch on Monday, but I want to see how they manage getting Penix up to full speed, and I know I’m not the only one who wants to know how he’s looking, so I’ll be there to keep y’all posted. All of my reporting from tomorrow’s practice will be in the Feed, and I’ll have a practice report on The Falcoholic afterward. Now let’s move on to everything you need to read, watch, or listen to about the Atlanta Falcons today. Josh Kendall of The Athletic shares his perspective on Saturday’s player performances and what they mean as we inch closer to roster cuts . Daniel Flick of the AJC introduces us to Za’Darius Smith , who didn’t join the Falcons in Indianapolis until Friday, but did immediately embrace being a part of this Falcons team. D. Orlando Ledbetter of Bowtie Sports has Kevin Stefanski’s full postgame press conference transcript from Saturday , in which the Falcons’ head coach discussed the improved performance of the o-line, gap integrity, Tyler Goodson, and more. I always think there’s value in reading the full transcript — if you just catch quotes here and there you may be missing important context. Candace Buckner of The Athletic wrote an outstanding piece after the Falcons’ joint practices last week about the Falcons’ QB1 conundrum , and it may be even more relevant now that Michael Penix Jr. has been medically cleared. ESPN ’s Mark Raimondi explains why the Falcons are so impressed with Jack Strand in the video below. View Link Falcons vs. Colts Preseason Week 2 coverage That Falcons win over the Colts was extremely fun. Relive it here . Dave Choate covers the snap counts from Saturday’s preseason win , right here on The Falcoh0lic. I am 100% in favor of taking cool-ass penalties on purpose in the preseason, like the excessive celebration flag against the Colts on Saturday. Safe to say the guys took it seriously 😂 pic.twitter.com/ka7HSl9CUv — Atlanta Falcons (@AtlantaFalcons) August 22, 2026 From The Falcoholic community On Friday, I asked everyone to write a mission statement for the 2026 Falcons. There were a ton of fun ones — I was especially partial to the thread that perfectly mimicked the cadence and tone of a certain politician’s Truth Social posts. Spot on, and legitimately hilarious! But TrenchesPlease had my absolute favorite: First of all, it’s an iconic line from an iconic Falcon. Secondly, I couldn’t agree more about the reasoning behind it. And I do think seeing the Falcons bounce back so dramatically on Day 2 of joint practices against the Colts and in Week 2 of the preseason after floundering Week 1 — these things should be indicative of better coaching and a better-run organization. I hope so, anyway. Join the conversation! Sign up for a user account and get: Fewer ads Create community posts Comment on articles, community posts Rec comments, community posts New, improved notifications system! The Falcoholic Question of the Day: Should Jack Strand be the Atlanta Falcons’ QB3 , or should it be Cooper Rush or someone else entirely — a trade, a waiver wire pickup, Matt Ryan comes out of retirement? Why do you think so? Let us know in the comments!

title: Falcons snap counts from a blowout preseason win over the Colts
summary: Snap counts, you say? Snap counts, I say. Here’s a quick breakdown of how the Falcons portioned out playing time yesterday in their preseason game against the Colts. Offense G Andrew Stueber: 55 G Kam Dewberry: 55 C James Brockermeyer: 49 WR Vinny Anthony: 46 QB Jack Strand: 44 T Ethan Onianwa: 41 G Brandon […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - AUGUST 22: Cash Jones #32 of the Atlanta Falcons celebrates after a touchdown during the preseason game against the Indianapolis Colts at Lucas Oil Stadium on August 22, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Chris Carter/Getty Images) | Getty Images Snap counts, you say? Snap counts, I say. Here’s a quick breakdown of how the Falcons portioned out playing time yesterday in their preseason game against the Colts. Offense G Andrew Stueber: 55 G Kam Dewberry: 55 C James Brockermeyer: 49 WR Vinny Anthony: 46 QB Jack Strand: 44 T Ethan Onianwa: 41 G Brandon Walton: 41 WR Dylan Drummond: 37 T Mike Jerrell: 37 TE Jack Velling: 36 WR Antwane Wells Jr.: 32 WR Chris Blair: 32 TE Josh Simon: 29 RB Cash Jones: 29 QB Cooper Rush: 29 RB Nate Carter: 28 TE Nick Muse: 28 WR Keelan Marion: 25 T Wanya Morris: 25 C Corey Levin: 24 G Kyle Hinton: 18 WR Beaux Collins: 17 RB Tyler Goodson: 16 G Jaeden Roberts: 13 T Riley Mahlman: 11 WR Zachariah Branch: 8 It was a much better day for the team’s cast of offensive linemen, with Onianwa and Jerrell going from active liabilities to solid contributors. It’s worth noting, too, that Corey Levin was once again with the second-string ahead of Brockermeyer (who also played better Saturday), and that undrafted free agent rookie Kam Dewberry drew the “start” and held his own at right guard. The worst day among any offensive linemen probably belonged to the veteran Stueber, who scuffled a bit and drew two holding penalties on one drive. In a crowded, competitive group vying for roles behind Jake Matthews, Matthew Bergeron, Ryan Neuzil, Chris Lindstrom, and Jawaan Taylor, standing out for good or ill could matter a lot. The same is true at wide receiver, where Blair continues to improve and show off a well-rounded skill set that should have him in the driver’s seat, especially given that he’s probably the best blocker in the group vying for roles. Blair helped himself that way in my estimation, while Anthony continues to look really good as a returner and quite capable as a receiving option. If the Falcons are going to keep four backs, I’m starting to believe Carter won’t be among them. He had a better day on Saturday than last Friday and is still a useful player the Falcons should plan to stash on the practice squad, but Goodson has pretty clearly been the better runner and is a more versatile player, while Jones looked explosive and capable as a receiving option out of the backfield. The best thing Strand could do was outperform Rush; the second best thing he could do was keep pace with him. The Falcons aren’t in a position to lose Strand, who looks far more talented and comfortable than we ever could’ve dreamed of coming into the spring, and if all things are roughly equal he’ll likely beat out Rush for a spot. Rush’s experience and proven history of stepping in will be attractive to the team given Michael Penix Jr.‘s injury history and Tua Tagovailoa’s injury concerns, but the upside seems higher for Strand and he will be snapped up if he lands on the practice squad. This is QB3 we’re talking about, so you can decide how much you care. Defense CB Clark Phillips III: 27 S DeMarcco Hellams: 27 CB CJ Henderson: 27 OLB Keshawn Banks: 24 OLB Azeez Ojulari: 24 DL Devonnsha Maxwell: 24 CB Cobee Bryant: 23 CB Malcolm DeWalt IV: 23 DB Natrone Brooks: 23 DL Chris Williams: 23 OLB James Pearce Jr.: 22 DL Carlos Allen Jr.: 22 OLB Cam Sample: 22 CB A.J. Woods: 19 S Jammie Robinson: 19 ILB Josh Woods: 19 DL Eric Johnson: 17 ILB Daveren Rayner: 16 ILB Channing Tindall: 16 CB Mike Ford: 16 LB Kendal Daniels: 15 ILB Christian Harris: 15 DL Zach Harrison: 15 S Sydney Brown: 15 S Keidron Smith: 12 CB Darren Hall: 12 ILB JD Bertrand: 11 ILB Harold Perkins Jr.: 8 CB Darnay Holmes: 8 DL Marlon Tuipulotu: 6 Kendal Daniels and JD Bertrand starting and Christian Harris getting into this game late feels like one of those things we could put too much stock in…but I’m going to do it, regardless. Daniels looked great again and was pulled early, and I have to think he’s at least going to be in a timeshare playing next to Divine Deablo to start the season. I planted my flag on this a while ago and I see no reason to back off it now; the bigger news would be if Bertrand had passed Harris on the pecking order. We’ll have to see if that holds up in the preseason finale, but given that Channing Tindall or Josh Woods is probably sticking around for his special teams value and the team clearly really likes Perkins, either Harris or Bertrand is probably going to be in a tough spot. At cornerback, Bryant had a bounceback game and DeWalt was quietly really good again, but it’s worth noting that Brooks and Henderson were deployed as starters. Henderson was penalized but otherwise looked solid, while Brooks turned in a customarily strong preseason performance, and if that’s the pecking order they probably will both make the roster with Aveion Terrell and Billy Bowman Jr. banged up. At safety, meanwhile, I have to think Hellams and Robinson have their spots locked up, and both turned in quality days again. Up front, it’s good news for Carlos Allen Jr. that he both started and had real fun moments as a pass rusher in this one. After an impressive week of practice against the Colts, he’s somebody who should be able to at least latch on to a practice squad spot. Special teams Jammie Robinson: 19 Channing Tindall: 16 Nick Muse: 15 Malcolm DeWalt IV: 14 Josh Woods: 14 Azeez Ojulari: 13 Nick Folk: 13 Clark Phillips III: 10 Keshawn Banks: 10 Cobee Bryant: 9 Tyler Goodson: 8 Liam McCullough: 8 Jake Bailey: 8 Jack Velling: 7 Harold Perkins Jr.: 7 Kendal Daniels: 7 JD Bertrand: 7 A.J. Woods: 7 CJ Henderson: 7 Kam Dewberry: 6 Daveren Rayner: 6 Chris Blair: 6 Keidron Smith: 6 Darren Hall: 6 Andrew Stueber: 6 Brandon Walton: 6 Dylan Drummond: 5 Mike Jerrell: 4 Vinny Anthony: 4 Ethan Onianwa: 4 Christian Harris: 4 Darnay Holmes: 4 Cash Jones: 3 Nate Carter: 3 Riley Mahlman: 3 Beaux Collins: 3 DeMarcco Hellams: 3 Chris Williams: 3 Corey Levin: 3 James Pearce Jr.: 2 Natrone Brooks: 2 Wanya Morris: 2 Sydney Brown: 2 Kyle Hinton: 2 Devonnsha Maxwell: 2 Mike Ford: 2 Zachariah Branch: 1 Keelan Marion: 1 Carlos Allen Jr.: 1 When you’re a borderline roster guy, you want to be the special team coordinator’s best friend. That’s why the heavy snap counts and quality performances for Robinson, DeWalt, Muse, Woods, and Tindall are really important. Tindall and Woods are effectively competing against one another for a roster spot, making those snaps incredibly valuable for both, while Robinson, DeWalt, and Muse could well beat out their competition (Robinson probably already has a leg up, but DeWalt is facing a spirited battle for a final cornerback spot and Muse needs to beat out Velling and Josh Simon) if they prove to be capable special teamers. I’d say you can safely book one of Woods/Tindall and Robinson in for spot already, based on who they’re competing against and their outsized roles here. Also, nice to have a super reliable kicker, isn’t it? So far Nick Folk has been nails.
author: Dave Choate

title: Falcons – Colts preseason recap: An unreserved beatdown from the reserves
summary: A game like this during the regular season would feed the Falcons fanbase for a long time. We’d crow over the result, allow it to dampen any roller coaster stretches that followed, and bring it up unprompted years later. Because it’s a preseason game, the glow won’t last nearly as long, but it still made […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - AUGUST 22: Tyler Goodson #25 of the Atlanta Falcons celebrates after a touchdown during the preseason game against the Indianapolis Colts at Lucas Oil Stadium on August 22, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Chris Carter/Getty Images) | Getty Images A game like this during the regular season would feed the Falcons fanbase for a long time. We’d crow over the result, allow it to dampen any roller coaster stretches that followed, and bring it up unprompted years later. Because it’s a preseason game, the glow won’t last nearly as long, but it still made for a very fine Saturday afternoon. After spirited joint practices earlier in the week where the Falcons starters turned in mixed efforts, the backups took the field and dominated Indianapolis start to finish. You need to stack the caveats like so many delicious pancakes—the Colts were running a vanilla game plan of their own, their quarterback situation is not superb, etc.—but it’s not like the Falcons were trotting out starters against backups or employing any exotic twists. This was just roster hopefuls against roster hopefuls, and our roster hopefuls kicked ass. You knew it was going to be a pretty good day when the Falcons kept forcing the Colts into costly mistakes and holds, and when they clamped down hard on Indy’s bruising runners. You knew it was going to be a great day when Cooper Rush came out firing and Jack Strand kept the good times rolling, and you knew it was going to be a superb day when Tyler Goodson rumbled for a 49 yard touchdown. It was so lopsided and so relatively free of huge problems and mistakes that the Ugly section of this article is going to be as short as it’s been in a long while, especially because I’m not keen to find tiny flaws in a preseason effort. It was also an excellent game for players the coaching staff wanted to see more from, ranging from Vinny Anthony to Strand to Kendal Daniels to Cam Sample. The staff will find more flaws and areas of improvement than we did from Saturday’s fesitivites, but I have to imagine they’re pleased by the caliber of performances and the way Mike Jerrell, Ethan Onianwa, Rush, and the pass rush bounced back after a rough effort against Denver. The full return of Michael Penix Jr. to practice will add more intrigue to the final week of preseason preparation, but there’s already plenty here to consider. This game does not—and should not—remove any and all concerns about how the starters looked against a game Broncos squad, or convince us that this team’s depth is light years ahead of where it was in the past. But it should absolutely makes us feel a bit better about the reserves and the state of the roster battles that are winding down right now, and after Week 2 of preseason, that’s good enough for me. Especially if it translates to better in-season outcomes when the team inevitably has to rely on that depth. On to the full recap. The Good This was a much better day for Cooper Rush, who had one weird skipped pass over the middle to Zachariah Branch early on but otherwise commanded the offense well, threw the ball effectively, and generally looked more like the guy who has been a useful NFL quarterback when called upon throughout his career. He needed this kind of effort to fend off Jack Strand, but… Jack Strand also looked terrific. He led two three scoring drives after entering the game, going 6 for his first 6 passes for 108 yards, including a deep ball to Antwane Wells Jr. and a touchdown to Cash Jones and finishing with over 200 yards on the day. He also cashed in his own touchdown from 20 yards on a scramble where he looked fast and decisive. It’s obvious that while Strand is not ready for primetime, he has enough talent to be a QB3 in this league easily , especially when you look around at who other teams are auditioning for their third spot. The Falcons have a tough decision ahead with two quarterbacks with injury issues atop the depth chart and the question of Rush’s experience versus Strand’s potential to answer, given that Strand may very well get snapped up off the team’s practice squad. Tyler Goodson just looks really good out there. Another couple of decisive runs on the first drive to turn nothing plays into solid gains made for a solid start, but then he uncorked a great kick return late in the first quarter, picking up 37 yards. He followed that up with the best play of preseason, rumbling for 49 yards after getting some nice blocks from Mike Jerrell and company and taking it to the house for a touchdown. The fact that he can do everything well and is running effectively in preseason should be enough to get him the RB3 job, and I feel great about this running back depth chart if he is. A word for Nate Carter, though, who looked better running the ball in this one and had a truly impressive play on third down in the second quarter where he stayed on his feet despite a huge fit near the goal line and powered his way in for a touchdown. Carter’s almost certainly making this practice squad unless someone the Falcons really like shakes loose at cutdown. Cash Jones also had a nice day on the ground, picking up multiple nine yard runs and reeling in a touchdown catch and a pair of nice fourth quarter catch and runs in the process. He exceeded that through the air, with a team-leading 4 catches (tied with Vinny Anthony), 62 yards, and a touchdown, I think Jones is probably ticketed for the practice squad, but he’s been good enough and has enough special teams value to push for a final roster spot. Man, the Falcons have a good problem at running back. There were some really promising performances from other pass catchers, as well. Anthony looked fluid and fast with the ball in his hands as a returner and receiver, Chris Blair continues to shine for what seems like the fifth straight preseason, both Beaux Collins and Antwane Wells Jr. made impressive plays, and tight ends Jack Velling and Nick Muse showed good hands. The team’s extreme depth issues at receiver in particular have hurt the Falcons in years past, but I’m cautiously optimistic of the options they have on hand between Anthony, Blair, and Wells. As you might guess by all the praise for playmakers, the offensive line was far better this week. I thought Mike Jerrell and Ethan Onianwa held their own, James Brockermeyer looked much less up-and-down than in his first professional action. A rewatch is a must to get a better sense of who truly stood out, but the Falcons only took one sack on the day and averaged over 4 yards per carry with deep reserves. The line earned its kudos. Carlos Allen Jr. has made the most of his opportunities this week, with big plays during joint practices and a near-sack on third down on Riley Leonard to stop a drive and make Indy settle for a field goal late in the first quarter. Chris Williams did not arrive in Atlanta with a reputation as a plus run defender, but there was some evident promise as a pass rusher to work with. Through two weeks of preseason, Williams has gotten close a handful of times and picked up a sack on Saturday, which can only help him cement a role up front in a rotation Nate Ollie wants constantly getting after the quarterback. I continue to be impressed by Kendal Daniels, who has shown the physicality promised by his college career and really good instincts to this point. Once again, he wore the green dot for the backup defense and was flying all over the field, with a highlight coming in the first quarter when he sniffed out a screen for zero gain. I remain convinced he’s either going to start or at least be heavily involved in Week 1. Both Christian Harris and Jammie Robinson had great pass breakups in this one, with Harris picking up a particularly emphatic swat that could’ve been an interception against Anthony Richardson late in this one. Nick Folk made his 51 yard field goal try in the first quarter look incredibly easy, drilling it right down the middle, and hit all his other kicks…

title: Buffalo Bills 53-man roster projection: After preseason victory over Browns
summary: The Buffalo Bills smoked the Cleveland Browns 31-7 in the preseason opener, a dominant effort by Joe Brady’s team from start to finish. With only one preseason game left before the Bills head to Houston to embark on their 2026 regular season, why not project the 53-man roster again? Technically, we do have new information […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - AUGUST 15: Ben VanSumeren #45 of the Buffalo Bills warms up prior to a preseason game against the Carolina Panthers at Highmark Stadium on August 15, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills smoked the Cleveland Browns 31-7 in the preseason opener, a dominant effort by Joe Brady’s team from start to finish. With only one preseason game left before the Bills head to Houston to embark on their 2026 regular season, why not project the 53-man roster again? Technically, we do have new information after Buffalo’s second exhibition victory. Quarterback (2) Josh Allen Kyle Allen Allen won the QB2 battle — a competition that did have some legs in training camp — with another surgical performance in the second preseason game. He’s not the best backup in the NFL but appears comfortable in Joe Brady’s system. Running Back (4) * James Cook Ray Davis Ian Wheeler Ben VanSumeren Johnson hurt his leg in the Return of the Blue and Red Scrimmage, and while the injuries weren’t related, also suffered an injury in the meaningless regular-season finale against the Jets last year which caused him to miss both of Buffalo’s playoff games. I mention that because playing without Johnson is a fresh memory for the Bills, and I’m sure they don’t want to experience that anymore. So, they opt to start Johnson on IR — thereby forcing him out of the first month of action — to give him plenty of time to get nursed back to full health. And, yes, for as good as Frank Gore Jr. has been for a third-straight preseason, he’s jumped by the bigger, more explosive Wheeler ahead of Week 1. Also, VanSumeren has already won the fullback battle. Now it’s just a matter of whether or not the Bills want to carry one on the roster. Now, I think they do. And he’s an obvious special-teamer. Wide Receiver (6) D.J. Moore Khalil Shakir Josh Palmer Keon Coleman Skyler Bell Trent Sherfield After consecutive weeks with seven receivers, I’m opting for six in this projection to make room at a few other positions. Buffalo is relatively banged up in their wideout room — like the club was for the majority of the 2025 campaign. And Sherfield’s strong showing against the Browns secures his spot on the roster as a special teams gunner with the ability to fill in at WR3 or WR4 if in a dire situation. And, yes, the Bills do feel thin at receiver, although Palmer’s summer is very encouraging. Tight End (3) Dalton Kincaid Dawson Knox Jackson Hawes Despite strong pushes by Keleki Latu and even Shane Zylstra, the Bills opt to keep their normal three tight ends on the roster. Do not sleep on Latu or even Zylstra getting practice-squad elevations this season. They’ve proven their worth this summer. Offensive Line (9) Dion Dawkins Alec Anderson Connor McGovern O’Cyrus Torrence Spencer Brown Austin Corbett Lloyd Cushenberry Tylan Grable Jude Bowry No changes here from a week ago. Anderson wins the left-guard job — barely — and Tylan Grable is the team’s swing tackle. Bowry has a long way to go in his development but clearly is being cross-trained at both tackle positions to eventually serve as the swing tackle if Grable moves into a starting role in the future. Look for Sedrick Van-Pran Granger to be a trade chip for Brandon Beane near cutdown day. Defensive Line (6) * Ed Oliver Deone Walker T.J. Sanders Landon Jackson Greg Gaines Zane Durant After the Gaines signing, the writing was on the wall for former third-round pick DeWayne Carter. Then he turned in a sound performance against the Browns in the second preseason game. The majority of his positive plays came in the fourth quarter, which was telling. Decisions will have to be made here with Mathis is ready to return from this three-game suspension. Inside Linebacker (4) Terrel Bernard Kaleb Elarms-Orr Dorian Williams Keonta Jenkins This position feels somewhat cemented right now — particularly after a strong performance from Jenkins in the preseason opener and another against the Browns. The real question with his position is how does Elarms-Orr fit into the normal rotation during the regular season? Rush Linebacker (6) Greg Rousseau Bradley Chubb Michael Hoecht T.J. Parker Javon Solomon Mike Danna After two sacks against the Panthers, Danna another pressure — a hit on Deshaun Watson that forced an incompletion. He was a pesky, dirty-work player for years in Kansas City and has the stocky body type to condense closer to the ball if needed in clear-cut passing situations. He’s a quality insurance option to have for Jim Leonhard’s multiple front. Defensive Backs (10) Christian Benford Maxwell Hairston Dee Alford Davison Igbinosun Cole Bishop CJ Gardner-Johnson Jordan Hancock Jalon Kilgore Kani Walker Sam Franklin Jr. I’ve gone back and forth on Damar Hamlin — he was an afterthought this offseason but has parlayed a strong camp into a solid preseason, and I do think in a perfect world, the Bills would like to keep him as veteran experience at safety behind Cole Bishop and CJ Gardner-Johnson. For this projection, he’s left off the 53-man roster with Buffalo hoping he can be stored on the practice squad. Specialists (3) Reid Ferguson Tommy Doman Jr. Tyler Bass Hard to say if there’s been a clear winner in the punter battle — as both Mitch Wishnowsky and Doman only got cracks at it in the second preseason game. This one could go down to the wire. *Phidarian Mathis will begin serving his three-game suspension at the start of the regular season so he will not originally be on the 53-man roster Week 1. *Ty Johnson begins the season on IR in this projection

title: Ed Oliver deserved the right to grieve his son privately
summary: Some stories are difficult to write because you struggle to find the right words. This is one of them. Buffalo Bills defensive tackle Ed Oliver and his family have been living through an unimaginable tragedy for nearly two months. Oliver’s 2-year-old son died on June 28 after being found unresponsive in a swimming pool at […]
full_text: Some stories are difficult to write because you struggle to find the right words. This is one of them. Buffalo Bills defensive tackle Ed Oliver and his family have been living through an unimaginable tragedy for nearly two months. Oliver’s 2-year-old son died on June 28 after being found unresponsive in a swimming pool at a residence outside Houston. According to reporting from ESPN’s Cameron Wolfe and Alaina Getzenberg, family members found the toddler, and he was transported by ambulance to a local hospital, where he was later pronounced dead. For nearly seven weeks, however, most of us knew none of this…and that was intentional. Some members of the Bills organization knew. Some of Oliver’s teammates knew. Some members of the media knew. And they kept it private. Not because there was some grand conspiracy or “media blackout.” Not because anyone was trying to hide something from Bills fans. They kept it private because a father had lost his child. Because Oliver and his family deserved the opportunity to process an unimaginable loss without thousands of strangers discussing it, dissecting it, speculating about it or demanding answers. That should have been enough. Oliver still showed up Perhaps one of the most heartbreaking details is something Bills fans had already witnessed without understanding what was happening behind the scenes: Oliver reported to training camp on time. Less than a month after losing his son, he arrived at St. John Fisher University and went back to work. He practiced. He spent time with his teammates. He participated throughout training camp and even played with Buffalo’s starters in the Bills’ preseason opener against the Carolina Panthers. Meanwhile, his teammates and the organization did exactly what Oliver apparently needed them to do: They gave him space, supported him, and allowed him to determine how he wanted to move forward. When Oliver later missed practices and did not travel to Cleveland for Buffalo’s second preseason game, his absence was attributed to an injury. The tragedy his family was carrying remained private. Until someone decided it shouldn’t. This wasn’t “his” story to tell On Friday, nearly seven weeks after Oliver’s son died, a person on X publicly connected Oliver to a June 28 news report involving the death of a toddler in Harris County, Texas. I’m intentionally not naming him here. He has received more than enough attention for taking something that wasn’t his to share and putting it into the public domain. Once the post began circulating, speculation exploded across social media. What Oliver, his family, his teammates and members of the media had managed to keep private for almost seven weeks suddenly became public conversation. That forced everyone else’s hand. ESPN’s Cameron Wolfe and Alaina Getzenberg subsequently confirmed the heartbreaking circumstances surrounding the death. The Bills organization, which had been aware of the tragedy since it occurred, then publicly acknowledged Oliver’s loss. General manager Brandon Beane released the following statement on behalf of the organization: “On behalf of the entire Buffalo Bills organization, we want to publicly express our condolences to Ed Oliver and his family on the devastating loss of his son. It’s an unthinkable tragedy for any parent. We will continue to support Ed and his family as we all grieve this tragic loss.” The organization had known and had been supporting him privately. Some reporters knew and chose not to publish it. They respected the wishes of a grieving family. There is something admirable about that, particularly in an era when being first too often seems more important than asking whether a story actually needs to be told. Josh Allen’s reaction said everything Following Buffalo’s second preseason victory on Saturday, Josh Allen was asked about his teammate. His response wasn’t just sadness. There was anger, too. “First off, I want to say thank you to the ones that knew about it and allowed him to have his moment and his time. It’s very sad in how it came out. It makes me very sad and angry at the same time. Obviously, very unfortunate what happened and as a teammate of him, as someone in this locker room, all we can do is love on him. There’s nothing that you can say to make the situation any better except being there in whatever ways he needs. That’s what we’re going to continue to do. That’s what teammates do. You love up on each other when we’re down, and I can’t imagine what he’s going through. But the way that he’s dealt with it has been unbelievable. Very, very unfortunate how it got out. As his teammates, that’s what we’ve been doing is giving him his space and time, but at the same time being around him, loving up on him, but not trying to do anything to reopen that. I understand lot of the guys in the locker room knew, especially on the D-line. He spends a lot of time with those guys, and everyone’s just rallying around him.” Allen acknowledged that not everyone inside the locker room knew what Oliver was going through. But for those who did, there appeared to be an understanding that this was Oliver’s story to tell, if and when he chose to tell it. Allen made that point very clear: “It’s the utmost, the most important thing, and I’m very … It’s just very unfortunate how it came about. I appreciate those that knew and didn’t want to bring it up… It’s no one’s place to really let that out there except him and his families when the time came for it, but we roll now and be there for him as teammates.” That last part matters : It was no one’s place. Professional athletes surrender an extraordinary amount of privacy when they choose this career. We discuss their contracts, their injuries, their performances, their mistakes, and sometimes their personal lives. But there should still be a line. The unexpected death of a child is well beyond it. Oliver didn’t owe us an announcement. He didn’t owe the media an explanation. He didn’t owe Bills Mafia a statement. He certainly didn’t owe strangers on social media access to the most painful experience imaginable simply because he plays football for a living. Bills Mafia responds the way Bills Mafia does Unfortunately, Oliver no longer gets to decide whether his loss is public. What Bills fans can decide is what they do with that knowledge…and Bills Mafia has already begun responding in a familiar way. Fans have started making donations in honor of Oliver and his family, many in increments of $9.10 or $91, a nod to Oliver’s No. 91 jersey. Two organizations have emerged as destinations for those donations: Coats for Kids in Western New York, which provides winter clothing to children in need throughout the Buffalo community, and Habitat for Horses , a Houston, Texas based horse protection organization. For fans who would like to participate: Coats for Kids WNY Habitat for Horses There have been countless moments over the years when Bills Mafia has turned tragedy into generosity. Donations don’t erase grief. They don’t fix what happened. They don’t make this loss any less devastating. But they can allow a community to say something without demanding anything in return. We’re here. We’re thinking about you. And you’re not walking through this alone. Some things are bigger than football Soon enough, we’ll go back to talking about football. We’ll analyze Oliver’s snaps, the positives, and negatives of his play. We’ll talk about his health, the Bills’ defensive front, wins and losses, and everything else that consumes an NFL season. Today doesn’t need to be about any of that. Today is about Ed Oliver the father, not Ed Oliver the football player. It’s about a locker room that quietly rallied around one of its own. An organization that respected his privacy. Reporters who knew something devastating and understood that knowing a story doesn’t automatically give you the right to tell it. And it’s about recognizing that Oliver and his family should have been allowed to decide when,…

title: 4 takeaways from Bills win over Browns in second preseason game
summary: The Buffalo Bills beat the Cleveland Browns 31-7 for the second straight resounding preseason win, and after the score was 7-7 in the first quarter — post-lightning delay — Joe Brady’s club dominated for the remainder of the game. You can read staffer what Sean Murphy’s wrote his stock up/stock down piece immediately following the […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - AUGUST 22: Ian Wheeler #27 of the Buffalo Bills runs the ball during the third quarter of a preseason game against the Cleveland Browns at Huntington Bank Field on August 22, 2026 in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills beat the Cleveland Browns 31-7 for the second straight resounding preseason win, and after the score was 7-7 in the first quarter — post-lightning delay — Joe Brady’s club dominated for the remainder of the game. You can read staffer what Sean Murphy’s wrote his stock up/stock down piece immediately following the victory, and Fernando Schmude posted his observational notebook from this contest. Check ‘em. These were my takeaways from this convincing Bills win. New developmental pieces are arriving During the Brandon Beane era, the Bills have done a remarkable job developing high-caliber talents who enter the league with raw skill sets. Look no further than Josh Allen. But Ed Oliver, Dawson Knox, Spencer Brown, Greg Rousseau, James Cook, and Cole Bishop are other examples of those project-y types who’ve blossomed within the Bills organization since arriving in Orchard Park. And the next wave is arriving. Landon Jackson, a 2025 selection that always felt like a pick for 2026, looks locked and loaded in the 4i – 5tech role. Not just larger, thicker, and ready for dirty work. But he maintained his explosiveness through his offseason body transformation — and remember, he ran 4.68 with a 40.5-inch vertical at 6’6” and 264 pounds at the 2025 NFL Combine. He’s officially a scary specimen for opposing offensive lines. T.J. Sanders, whom I wrote about as the ultimate X-factor on this year’s Buffalo defense, looks more motivated and with more pop in his hands than a season ago. Even Jordan Hancock, who was probably the least project-y of this youth movement on defense because of all the hats he wore at Ohio State, appears primed to be a magnet to the football with his 4.46 speed and 41.5-inch vertical explosiveness. Don’t sleep on new swing tackle Tylan Grable, Jalon Kilgore, Keleki Latu, or rookie Ar’maj Reed-Adams either. After a marvelous 2022 draft class that featured Cook, Terrel Bernard, Khalil Shakir, and Christian Benford, the Bills’ clear hits had been a bit more spotty. But with the new upside-based projects starting to arrive, those drafting perceptions will change in 2026. The Bills are suddenly loaded at RB and TE Sure, they were working against backups in Cleveland on Saturday, but they too, are backups, and were on the field with Bills backups — Buffalo’s running backs were sensational in the team’s second preseason game. As a longtime advocate of waiting for running backs in the draft, because of the surplus of capable talents available on Day 3 I’m certainly convinced that if Phillip Wheeler needed to take regular-season carries behind the Bills starting offensive line he could be perfectly fine as a complementary piece to the club’s run game. The same goes for Frank Gore Jr. Wheeler has forced five missed tackles on 21 preseason attempts to date — good for a 23.8% missed tackle forced rate, and anything above 20% is high-end for a running back. He also has a pair of 10-plus yard runs and a hefty 3.24 yards-after-contact-per-rush average. Gore has forced six missed tackles on just 16 attempts, good for a 37.5% MTF rate. He has three runs of 10 or more yards. I went into the training camp with a low-key concern about the depth in Buffalo’s backfield. That concern has vanished. Seriously. If they’re called upon this season — either from the 53-man roster or via practice-squad elevation, these two will be ready. The same goes for the tight end group, although with Dalton Kincaid, Knox, and Jackson Hawes, we all presumed the Bills were deep at that position. But as it currently stands, Keleki Latu and even Shane Zylstra have done enough to legitimately deepen Buffalo’s tight-end room. Zylstra had three snags for 29 yards — that featured 13 yards after the catch and two first downs — against the Browns, and for the second-straight week, was a ferocious blocker for the run and pass game. Latu blocked his behind off against the Panthers and was a formidable edge-protecting presence in pass protection against Cleveland. Plus, at north of 6’6” and 250-plus pounds, he’s actually most tantalizing as a receiver. There’s more diversity to this Bills offense Of course Brady wasn’t showing anything remotely close to his full hand during the preseason, yet what he has shown has been an impressive array of pre-snap alignments and play-calling. Kyle Allen’s utilized play-action on just over 31% of his drop backs. Shane Buechele’s thrown off play-action 52.4% of the time, and five of Josh Allen’s nine drop backs featured play-action. HELLO. And many of these play-action drop backs have come from under center. We’ve seen jet sweeps. Jumbo looks. Gap-scheme running. Outside zone. Tunnel screens. Pitch plays. Outside screens. Deep overs. Shot plays down the sideline. More usage of the middle of the field at the intermediate level. I don’t want to attempt to glean too much from these first two preseason games from a schematic offensive perspective, but assuming there’s been little to no game-planning, and we’ve only gotten a sliver of Brady’s full-scale offense, I’m confident venturing a guess the Bills will be throwing the kitchen sink at opposing defenses this season. Buffalo’s run fits on defense feel more urgent and fundamentally sound The Bills have surrendered 3.1 yards per carry in consecutive preseason games. Yes, it’s just the preseason, but in watching the film, Buffalo’s run-defense unit feels noticeably more buttoned up and faster to the football from all 11 players on the field. I can’t say I know all the intricacies of Jim Leonhard’s run-defensive philosophy and how he coaches it differently than Sean McDermott or any of theBills defensive coordinators during the McDermott era. But I have a hunch Leonhard’s public comments about the seriousness of tackling reliability have something to do with it, and I’ll certainly be tracking this during the regular season. In 2025, the Bills averaged 8.8 missed tackles per game during the regular season. They were credited with seven missed tackles against the Panthers and just four against the Browns. Of course, individuals make tackles, and many of the players who saw the field in Cleveland for both the Bills and Browns won’t be playing much — if at all — once the regular season arrives. But collectively I’ve noticed fewer out-of-control tackling attempts and more defenders getting squared up with their ball-carrying targets. And Buffalo’s defensive front, distinctly playing more read-and-react than past iterations, has been noticeably more difficult for running backs to find creases through.

title: Kyle Allen quiets his doubters against the Cleveland Browns
summary: One of the ongoing storylines around the Buffalo Bills this offseason has focused on the backup for quarterback Josh Allen. It is understandable that this is an important topic to fans, as Allen is considered the top quarterback in the NFL. The club knew they would have a new backup in place after Mitchell Trubisky […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - AUGUST 22: Kyle Allen #11 of the Buffalo Bills throws a pass during the second quarter of a preseason game against the Cleveland Browns at Huntington Bank Field on August 22, 2026 in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Getty Images) | Getty Images One of the ongoing storylines around the Buffalo Bills this offseason has focused on the backup for quarterback Josh Allen. It is understandable that this is an important topic to fans, as Allen is considered the top quarterback in the NFL. The club knew they would have a new backup in place after Mitchell Trubisky signed with the Tennessee Titans. Brandon Beane opted to have a familiar face return to Buffalo, with the signing of Kyle Allen. While the 30-year old journeyman played with the Bills in 2023, there were plenty of questions if he was an adequate backup for the team. An uneven training camp certainly added fuel to the fire, that had many questioning – myself included – if the Bills needed to find a more capable back-up. Thankfully for the Bills, and their fans, Allen put those questions to rest with his performance on Saturday. As expected, Kyle Allen got the starting nod on Saturday as most of the starters received a day off. Allen was effective and efficient on the day, completing 10 of 12 attempts for 128 yards. He led the Bills to two scoring drives on the day, and led a successful two-minute drill to end the half with a touchdown pass to Mecole Hardman. Allen connected with Trent Sherfield four times on the day for a total of 54 yards – boosting his roster chances as well. Now that Allen has played two successful preseason games this season (completing 24 of 28 attempts), I hope that Bills fans can relax a bit when it comes to the back-up quarterback. I just hope that we do not need to see Allen take the field this season, unless it is in garbage time of a Bills blowout victory.

title: Bills news: Recapping Bills vs. Browns
summary: It appears the competition to claim the backup quarterback job behind Josh Allen is settled for the Buffalo Bills, as veteran Kyle Allen has posted back-to-back efficient performances this preseason for the Bills. Today’s edition of Buffalo Rumblinks leads off by recapping Kyle Allen’s strong outing in leading Buffalo to its second straight preseason win […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - AUGUST 22: Kyle Allen #11 of the Buffalo Bills throws a pass during the first quarter of a preseason game against the Cleveland Browns at Huntington Bank Field on August 22, 2026 in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images It appears the competition to claim the backup quarterback job behind Josh Allen is settled for the Buffalo Bills, as veteran Kyle Allen has posted back-to-back efficient performances this preseason for the Bills. Today’s edition of Buffalo Rumblinks leads off by recapping Kyle Allen’s strong outing in leading Buffalo to its second straight preseason win and examining which players are on the rise and who saw their stock take a hit in Week 2 of the preseason. Check out the assessments below and then let us know your thoughts on the game in the comments section. Observations and standouts from Buffalo’s 31-7 win over Cleveland Backup quarterback Kyle Allen has made the most of his preseason opportunities, turning in two impressive performances in wins over the Carolina Panthers and Cleveland Browns. On Saturday, in Buffalo’s second preseason contest, Allen might have clinched the backup job, completing 10 of 12 passes for 128 yards and a nine-yard touchdown pass to Mecole Hardman Jr. right before the end of the first half as the Bills took a 14-7 lead into halftime. Allen lofted a perfect deep ball to receiver Ja’Mori Maclin for a 37-yard gain that set up the Allen to Hardman score, who continued his strong preseason by catching a pair of passes for 108 yards in the win, while Ian Wheeler (56 yards) and Frank Gore Jr. (54 yards) combined to rush for 110 yards on their 23 carries, though Gore did have a fumble. Damar Hamlin and Te’Cory Couch (pictured below) each added interceptions as Jim Leonhard’s defense held the Browns scoreless over the final 48 minutes of the game. What else stood out from the win? Defensive end Landon Jackson was a disruptive force in the backfield; rookie outside linebacker had several impressive pass-rushing reps; cornerback Jordan Hancock came up with a huge pass breakup on a third-down play; veteran Trent Sherfield caught all four of his targets for 54 yards and was Buffalo’s best receiver in the first half; left guard Alec Anderson earned the first-team reps over Austin Corbett; and Hamlin led the team with five tackles to go with his interception. title: Buffalo Bills 2026 scouting report: kicker Tyler Bass
summary: The Buffalo Bills used multiple kickers last season thanks to a variety of injuries at the position. For the majority of the season, it was veteran Matt Prater handling the duties, and the 41-year old was fantastic. He hit on 90% of his tries during the regular season, nailing 18-of-20 field goals over the course […]
full_text: Bills kicker Tyler Bass kicks off during drills. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Buffalo Bills used multiple kickers last season thanks to a variety of injuries at the position. For the majority of the season, it was veteran Matt Prater handling the duties, and the 41-year old was fantastic. He hit on 90% of his tries during the regular season, nailing 18-of-20 field goals over the course of 15 games. He did miss time thanks to a quad injury, but he returned in time for the postseason. Prater made all five of his field goal tries and all six of his extra points. Michael Badgley also kicked in two games for the Bills, and while he made his only field goal try, it was his PAT misses that led to his dismissal. Even running back Ray Davis had a go, as he made an extra ppoint during the preseason and attempted an onside kick during the regular season. It’s unlikely that any of the aforementioned players will attempt a kick for Buffalo this season, as the man whom the team expected to handle the kicking last year is now back and available. In today’s installment of our “91 players in 91 days” series, we discuss the only kicker on Buffalo’s current roster. _____________________________________________________________________________ Name: Tyler Bass Number: 16 Position: K Height/Weight: 5’10” 183 lbs. Age: 29 (30 on 2/114/2027) Experience/Draft: 7; selected by Buffalo in the sixth round (No. 188 overall) of the 2020 NFL Draft College: Georgia Southern Acquired: Sixth-round draft choice Financial situation (per Spotrac): Bass signed a renegotiated two-year deal worth $6.75 million this offseason. His cap hit is $3.05 million if he makes the 53-man roster, and Buffalo will carry a dead cap charge of $2.54 million if he’s released. 2025 Recap: Bass underwent core muscle surgery in the offseason, though the extent of his injuries didn’t become known until December. He missed the entire season as he recovered from that surgery. Buffalo placed Bass on injured reserve on September 5. They had signed Prater to replace him the day prior. Positional outlook: Bass is the only kicker on Buffalo’s current roster. Maddux Trujillo had been in camp, but the Bills released him on May 12. 2026 Offseason: Bass has mostly kicked away from reporters and fans during camp, which led to some speculation regarding his health. At his first public kicking practice, though, he was perfect on seven tries . He also looked good kicking inside Highmark Stadium for the first time a few days later. 2026 Season outlook: Bass is Buffalo’s kicker, and while the renegotiated contract gives the team some wiggle room, it’s still unlikely that they release him barring catastrophic failure on his part. Prior to the injury, Bass was solid but inconsistent. Kicking in the wind tunnel that was the old Highmark Stadium (or Rich Stadium, or Ralph Wilson Stadium, or New Era Field—take your pick) might have contributed to that inconsistency. The wind inside the new stadium is said to be much less of a factor at field level, though we’ll see how that holds up when it’s 10 degrees and the wind is blowing snow off of Lake Erie in December. Prater was nearly automatic last season, so Bass does have some pressure to live up to the veteran’s success. Hopefully, he’s reayd to roll almost immediately. I anticipate that the Bills will try some field goals in preseason games where they might go for conversions on fourth down if it were the regular season. That way, they can ease their kicker back into game-like action. They’re going to need him to make a big kick at some point, and they need to make sure that he’s in a place to do that both physically and mentally. When the team fires up the Bass-o-Matic, they need to know it’ll function the right way. Thus far, Bass has looked like his old self. Let’s hope that continues when the games matter.

title: Fernando’s Notebook: Bills win in 31-7 rout over Browns in preseason game No. 2
summary: The Bills beat the Browns 31-7 in Saturday’s preseason Week 2 game in Cleveland, and this could be a new recurring format for me (as long as you enjoy it), post games — live notes from the broadcast, shared as-is, no full breakdown. Here’s what stood out to me watching the Bills’ second preseason game, […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - AUGUST 22: Damar Hamlin #3 of the Buffalo Bills celebrates after intercepting a pass during the second quarter of a preseason game against the Cleveland Browns at Huntington Bank Field on August 22, 2026 in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Bills beat the Browns 31-7 in Saturday’s preseason Week 2 game in Cleveland, and this could be a new recurring format for me (as long as you enjoy it), post games — live notes from the broadcast, shared as-is, no full breakdown. Here’s what stood out to me watching the Bills’ second preseason game, let me know your opinions in the comments section. Offense Trent Sherfield looks way bigger than in his first stint with the Bills, maybe the result of shifting his focus to special teams play. However, he looks like a guy who could also grow on that Mack Hollins/Tyrell Shavers role on offense, doing the dirty work and catching some important passes here and there. Ray Davis looks good, a real pro. He’s not awesome at anything (other than kick returning), but he’s good at everything. Kinda like poor man’s Fred Jackson. Rookie OT Jude Bowry continues to struggle. When the Bills drafted him early in Round 4, I hoped he could be a factor being kicked inside and competing for the LG job, but it never happened. As a pure OT, right now, Grable is light years ahead of him. Hopefully Grable can stay healthy. Kyle Allen has done everything right to guarantee that QB2 job. He can operate efficiently from the pocket and has a better arm, size, and experience in comparison to Buechele. Alec Anderson hasn’t opened the door for Corbert at LG; I think he’ll win the job. Good to have a veteran like Corbert as a plan B, though. Nice 2-min drive to close the 1st half. People poke fun at Brady’s screens, but I love them. When well executed by the players, they result in easy gains. Ja’Mori Maclin took advantage of his opportunities today. Always a threat down the field and could capitalize with a great catch on a deep pass from Kyle Allen and showing some burst after the catch on his TD from Shane Buechele. PS bound? Ja’Mori Maclin took advantage of his opportunities today. Always a threat down the field and could capitalize with a great catch on a deep pass from Kyle Allen and showing some burst after the catch on his TD from Shane Buechele. It’s a crowded WR room, PS bound? Ian Wheeler is an interesting back. More athletic than Gore, seems like a guy who could do some damage behind our starting OL. Our top 3 seems locked, but Wheeler is really intriguing, and Ty Johnson didn’t play at the same level in 2025 as he did in 2024. He has a clear 3rd down role, though. Frank Gore Jr. can play. He lacks top-notch athleticism, but his vision and balance are really good. Nice couple of moves to make some defenders miss in the 4th qrtr. Shane Buechele can move better than Kyle Allen and create a bit out of the structure. Those are some points that gotta be considered when evaluating a backup to Josh. I’d still go with KA, though. Defense Kani Walker reminds me of rookie Christian Benford. Good size, poised, can tackle, and knows where he’s supposed to be, vs run and pass. TJ Sanders is in position to start but hasn’t done anything yet to prove he deserves this role. As a former 2nd-round pick who the Bills traded up for, I expected more from him in his rookie season, and it didn’t happen. Year 2 hasn’t started any better. He flashed in a couple of plays, but it isn’t enough; I need to see more from him. Landon Jackson is another guy I’ve been worried about. Hated the pick but, with the scheme change and the new role, I actually have some hope for him now. He might give Sanders a run for his money. Davison Igbinosun is another guy who might find himself in the starting lineup soon, and I believe once he gets there, he might be able to secure that spot permanently. He’s big, physical, can tackle, and fits Leonhard’s schemes well. I love Max Hairston and hope he becomes a star, but how fragile he’s been is worrisome. Kaleb Elarms-Orr looks the part as an MLB — big, fast, physical. I’d love to see him beating Dorian Williams for a starting spot (Dorian’s contract is up after this year), but, unfortunately, he seems out of position way too often, especially when in coverage. On Cleveland’s first TD, he literally covered the same short area Damar Hamlin was covering, allowing a huge line to the wide-open receiver on the back of the end zone. I have to rewatch the play, but it seemed he should be better positioned to avoid that from happening. If TJ Parker learns some tricks from Bradley Chubb, he’ll be a problem. He’s very active and has a nice combo of speed/power. Gotta add moves to his arsenal. I like Jordan Hancock better at NCB. He looks good closer to the LOS than as a single high safety. Damar Hamlin can’t be a starter; he’s too slow. However, he’s a true pro who knows where he’s supposed to be, isn’t afraid of tackling (of all people), and continues to be rewarded for all those valuable traits. Geno Stone is also too slow. He isn’t a good tackler but always has been a ball hawk. Not with the Bills yet. Javon Solomon looks much better in a 5-man front. Nuff said. Mike Danna establishes a very solid floor in this OLB group. I liked what I saw from Buffalo Joe. He definitely outplayed Keonta Jenkins and, to be honest, he wasn’t worse than Dorian Williams or Kaleb Elarms-Orr. Special Teams Tommy Doman looks good. Wishnowsky was rock solid last year, but I think Buffalo has found its long-term answer at the position. I’m really uncomfortable with Tyler Bass at the moment. I’d go with Matt Prater this season again. Hopefully they really know what they’re doing there. Ray Davis returning punts is intriguing. I’d like to see him winning the job and becoming our answer in the return game overall. However, I feel like Kick and punt returns are way too different nowadays, and probably a shiftier guy would be a better option as the PR. As long as he shows he’s dependable enough catching those punts, though, he should be fine. Not About the Bills but… Did “The Monstars” steal Deshaun Watson’s talent? My goodness, dude was one of the top young QBs in the league and now looks nothing like his former self. Catch up on all this and more with the latest edition of Leading the Charge!

title: 2026 Season Opener Countdown: 21 Days Remaining
summary: Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NC - JANUARY 03: Charles Johnson #95 of the Carolina Panthers reacts after a play during their NFC Wild Card Playoff game against the Arizona Cardinals at Bank of America Stadium on January 3, 2015 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Streeter Lecka/Getty Images) | Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #21. Charles Johnson The Carolina Panthers have a pretty storied history of pass rushers. One of the most understated but effective nonetheless was Charles Johnson, who was a cornerstone of the defensive line in the 2010s. The Panthers were able to nab Johnson in the middle of the third round, which was seen by many as a steal at the time. He had to wait his turn though. He joined a loaded defensive line in Carolina that heavily relied on Julius Peppers and Mike Rucker at defensive end, which left little room for Johnson to make an impact. Rucker retired after the season, but the Panthers attempted to replace him in free agency with Tyler Brayton. Johnson was able to see more time in the field behind a less decorated starter, and he started to make his presence felt. He totaled ten sacks in those two years in a rotational role. He finally earned the opportunity to start after Julius Peppers departed in free agency. Johnson was never going to be Julius Peppers, but he did ease the sting a little bit from Peppers’ departure. He notched 11.5 sacks in his first season as a starter and followed that with totals of 9, 12.5, 11, and 8.5 in the next four seasons. There wasn’t a lot of flash to his game. He was a pure bull rusher, but he was able to rely on his strength to disrupt the pocket and finish plays. His rush style also kept him well positioned to defend the run, making him an ideal every down lineman. In 2015, Johnson missed nearly half the season with a severe hamstring injury. He saw his production take a major hit, even after his return, though he was able to register a sack in each of the Panthers’ three playoff games that season. He was released after that season for cap purposes but re-signed a few days later. He would spend the next two seasons in Carolina in a more limited role before retiring after the 2017 season. Johnson was not a flashy player in any way. He was a quiet mannered person and didn’t have a lot of pizzaz to his game, but that was never a detriment to his effectiveness. He was extraordinarily consistent both as a pass rusher and a run stopper and rarely missed a game. He played his entire career in Carolina and tallied 67.5 sacks during his time. That’s second most in Panthers history. For that, he lands at number 21 on the list of top 100 Carolina Panthers of all time.

Josh Sunderbruch: Jamree Kromah played with urgency and some power, and he showed the spark the DL has been lacking. Lester A.
