title: What Lions vs. Commanders snap counts tell us about Detroit’s roster
summary: How the Detroit Lions utilize their players in the preseason can often tell us a lot about their intentions when it comes to next week’s roster cuts. It’s not only how much you play, but what order the players take the field, and you can never forget special teams. So let’s take a closer look […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - AUGUST 22: Trayveon Williams #47 and Joshua Dobbs #6 of the Detroit Lions celebrate after Williams scored a touchdown during the third quarter of a preseason game against the Washington Commanders at Ford Field on August 22, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Nic Antaya/Getty Images) | Getty Images How the Detroit Lions utilize their players in the preseason can often tell us a lot about their intentions when it comes to next week’s roster cuts. It’s not only how much you play, but what order the players take the field, and you can never forget special teams. So let’s take a closer look at the Detroit Lions’ snap count from their preseason game against the Washington Commanders and dive into what it may mean for roster construction. Quarterbacks: Luke Altmyer: 38 snaps (57%) Josh Dobbs: 29 (43%) Jared Goff: DNP Josh Dobbs got the start, despite getting very little reps during training camp. Though his afternoon got off to a disastrous start, he eventually settled in and helped orchestrate both Lions touchdown drives, including a 50-yard rushing touchdown of his own. Luke Altmyer rotated in with Dobbs and never made any huge mistakes like Dobbs’ two turnovers, but only managed to headman a single scoring drive. I don’t think Saturday’s game gave us any true hints as to where the backup battle currently stands. Running backs: Trayveon Williams: 22 (33%) — 1 special teams snap (5%) Jacob Saylors: 20 (30%) — 4 (18%) Raheem Blackshear: 19 (28%) — 4 (18%) Jabari Small: 6 (9%) — 1 (5%) Jahmyr Gibbs: DNP Isiah Pacheco: DNP (injury) Sione Vaki: DNP (injury) While Vaki’s injury held him out of Saturday’s game, coach Dan Campbell’s encouraging words about him all but lock in a roster spot for him—despite his constant battles through injury. Unfortunately, injury may keep Jabari Small from making the team. He missed the first preseason game with an injury and after just six snaps against the Commanders, he was pulled to enter concussion protocol. Campbell had previously mentioned how Small and Jacob Saylors were neck-and-neck in a potential RB4 competition, but this concussion could be the tipping point. Elsewhere, Raheem Blackshear and Trayveon Williams impressed in a lot of reserve duty. While it’ll be hard for each to contend for a 53-man roster spot, both helped their case to stick around on the practice squad—particularly Williams. Wide receivers: Tay Martin: 31 (46%) — 6 (27%) Isaac TeSlaa: 27 (40%) Tarik Black: 24 (36%) — 6 (27%) Lucky Jackson: 24 (36%) — 4 (18%) Malik Cunningham: 14 (21%) Dominic Lovett: 14 (21%) Tom Kennedy: 7 (10%) — 6 (27%) Greg Dortch: 7 (10%) — 3 (14%) Cedrick Wilson: 5 (7%) Amon-Ra St. Brown: DNP Jameson Williams: DNP In terms of overall results, Tay Martin’s day was mixed. But the fact that he started the game and played a lot on special teams is quite telling that he’s likely the leading candidate for the WR5 job, especially after Cedrick Wilson’s injury, which Campbell expressed fear that it could be serious . Martin had a key drop on third down, but Campbell said there were good things that Martin did that went overlooked, too. “I don’t feel like this is something where, ‘Man, he’s had these glowing opportunities that he didn’t capitalize on.’ I don’t feel that way at receiver. I feel like he’s made a couple of plays that were there, really hadn’t got – now listen, I will tell you, there were two plays today where his number was called for an explosive, and he’s open, and we didn’t get it there.” He also mentioned Martin drew a special teams penalty. On the opposite end of the spectrum, it certainly isn’t a good sign that 2025 draft pick Dominic Lovett had a decreased role and zero reps on special teams. He did haul in a catch for 6 yards, but that’s hardly enough of an impact for a player who isn’t contributing on teams. Meanwhile, it’s a bit disappointing to see TeSlaa play that much and not garner a single target from either quarterback. Still, the reps are important even when the ball isn’t coming his way. Tight ends: Tyler Gordon: 28 (42%) — 5 (23%) Jackson Meeks: 28 (42%) — 10 (45%) Tyler Conklin: 27 (40%) — 4 (18%) Zach Horton: 20 (30%) — 2 (9%) Brock Wright: 12 (18%) — 3 (14%) Sam LaPorta: DNP (injury) Jackson Meeks was arguably the biggest winner of the game. He played a ton on Saturday, including 10 special teams snaps, which was the most of any player on offense. His forced fumble on kickoff duties essentially sealed the game for Detroit. Campbell praised Meeks after the game, but preached patience with him as he continues to learn nuances to the new tight end position. “He’s strong and he’s willing. And he’s smart,” Campbell said. “So, it’s just time on task. He’s another one, but you see how he attacks special teams. He gives our guys fits and special teams, too. Some of these looks, whether he’s on that team, or he’s giving—say I’m on the opposite of the ball and we’re on punt and I’m on punt rush, he will just give our guys fits. So that was good to see. I thought he did some really good things today. He made some critical plays.” If there will be a TE4 on the roster, Meeks has to be the leading candidate behind Sam LaPorta, Brock Wright, and Tyler Conklin. Offensive tackle: Miles Frazier: 48 (72%) — 2 (9%) Colby Sorsdal: 46 (69%) — 2 (9%) Devin Cochran: 26 (39%) Blake Miller: 15 (22%) — 2 (9%) Larry Borom: 15 (22%) — 2 (9%) Penei Sewell: DNP Frazier played both tackle spots and right guard on Saturday, as he continues to flash his versatility. That was certainly helpful on Saturday, and you’d have to imagine Detroit would appreciate that during the regular season—particularly as they struggle with the health of their depth players (see: Bartch, Niese, Mays). Not much else to note about this group, as the tackle room seems fairly straightforward when building the roster. Penei Sewell, Larry Borom, and Blake Miller are locks. And Frazier as a versatile depth piece is likely the only other one to make the roster—although it was good to see Devin Cochran out there, as he’s battled injury for nearly all camp. Guard/center: Mason Miller: 52 (78%) — 2 (9%) Seth McLaughlin: 51 (76%) — 4 (18%) Melvin Priestly: 36 (54%) — 2 (9%) Christian Mahogany: 15 (22%) — 4 (18%) Juice Scruggs: 15 (22%) — 2 (9%) Tate Ratledge: 15 (22%) — 2 (9%) Michael Niese: 1 (1%) Ben Bartch: DNP (injury) Cade Mays: DNP (injury) Interestingly, after playing solely right guard in the preseason opener, Mason Miller played strictly left guard against the Commanders. With some questions about the depth at guard, showcasing that versatility could give him a leg up if Detroit opts to part ways with the oft-injured Ben Bartch. Seth McLaughlin played a ton in this game, but unfortunately, that was due to third-string center Michael Niese suffering an injury on his one and only play. McLaughlin struggled quite a bit in the second half, which likely created more distance between him and presumed starter Juice Scruggs (with Cade Mays out). Semi-interesting note: the Lions opted to throw Christian Mahogany out there on special teams to replace Niese’s role. Defensive end: Derrick Moore: 25 (52%) — 4 (18%) Ahmed Hassanein: 19 (40%) — 2 (9%) DJ Wonnum: 14 (29%) — 1 (5%) Anthony Lucas: 13 (27%) Eric O’Neill: 9 (19%) Tyler Lacy: 7 (15%) — 2 (9%) Aidan Hutchinson: DNP Payton Turner: DNP (injury) First of all, I think it’s worth pointing out just how few snaps there were to go around on defense. Detroit only played 48 total snaps on that side of the ball, compared to 67 on offense. So as you’ll see, a lot of reserves didn’t get much time. As an example, the Commanders ran a total of just nine plays in the fourth quarter. So Eric O’Neill and Anthony Lucas felt the brunt of that bad luck. And while O’Neill continues to make the most of his opportunities, it does speak loudly that he’s not repping until late in the game. Meanwhile, Detroit loaded Derrick Moore’s plate in his NFL debut, and the rookie delivered a solid performance. It was also…

title: 5 Detroit Lions who hurt their roster chances vs. Washington Commanders
summary: Even though the stakes of a preseason game are low, a win feels good nonetheless. The Detroit Lions defeated the Washington Commanders in their second preseason game with a modest 17-13 score line. There has been promise on both sides of the ball, but an equal number of questions still up in the air. A […]
full_text: DETROIT,MICHIGAN-AUGUST 22: Detroit Lions quarterback Joshua Dobbs (6) goes to pass the ball during the second half of an NFL preseason football game between the Washington Commanders and the Detroit Lions in Detroit, Michigan USA, on Saturday, August 22, 2026 (Photo by Amy Lemus/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images Even though the stakes of a preseason game are low, a win feels good nonetheless. The Detroit Lions defeated the Washington Commanders in their second preseason game with a modest 17-13 score line. There has been promise on both sides of the ball, but an equal number of questions still up in the air. A fair number of Lions starters saw action on Saturday, yet that was more of a tune up for the regular season. Where things got interesting was the state of the reserves. Some of them mixed in with starters, while others only got late-game snaps. Regardless of when they entered the game, these backups played like their jobs depended on it—because it did. Which players took a hit to their stock after the Commanders game? Previously: 5 Lions who helped their roster chances vs. Commanders Seth McLaughlin, C McLaughlin had an impressive preseason debut against the Cincinnati Bengals last week, but his game took a notable step back against the Commanders. Washington’s interior was giving him fits throughout the game through a speed, power, or a combination of both. While he was only credited with allowing one sack, he did a subpar job keeping the pocket clean for either Joshua Dobbs or Luke Altmyer as both quarterbacks were forced outside far too many times. Worse yet for McLaughlin, he had a string of bad penalties that would normally kill a drive. On third-and-5, he double clutched a snap which led to a false start by Miles Frazier, then subsequently false started himself on the next play. The Lions lucked out with a 20-yard defensive pass interference penalty on the ensuing play, but that does not excuse the mistakes—turning a third-and-short into third-and-long is something that cannot happen. McLaughlin saw a sizeable number of snaps due to Michael Niese’s injury , so he will likely hang onto the backup center position behind Juice Scruggs if Niese misses time. However, given how perilous his roster spot is, he needs a rebound in the Lions’ final preseason game. Because Tate Ratledge could be a game-day emergency center, having a backup on the active roster is not a pressing need—McLaughlin has to earn it. Joshua Dobbs, QB Last week, I said that Luke Altmyer’s roster chances took a hit because he failed to capitalize on an opportunity to elevate himself in the QB2 battle. This week, I will ding Dobbs for a similar reason. While credited with two turnovers, the only one that was truly his fault was the interception. However, that interception was an absolute mess. Despite good protection from the offensive line, Dobbs had happy feet and wound up rolling outside the pocket. He stopped, planted, and pulled the trigger on a cross-body pass with a rusher in his face and sailed it into the arms of a defender. To add insult, he had Tay Martin wide open underneath (in his field of view as well) and could have connected for an easy first down—additionally, Martin’s nearest defender was a linebacker, so he had the matchup advantage to turn it into an even bigger gain. A veteran should not be making decisions like that. Dobbs redeemed himself with a 50-yard touchdown run (with Martin and Tyler Conklin providing pivotal blocks to spring him) on the next drive, flashing his elite athleticism. That being said, his ability as a runner was always a known commodity. I was personally hoping to see more from him as a passer, and his production thus far has been modest. Through two games, neither Dobbs nor Altmyer have seized the backup quarterback spot. As I mentioned in my 53-man roster prediction , because Dobbs is not subject to waivers, there is a chance that the Lions opt to keep Altmyer and sign Dobbs to the practice squad risk-free (unless he signs elsewhere, of course). If neither quarterback takes the lead, that could be the deciding factor for who makes the initial roster—the margins are that slim. Nick Whiteside, CB The bar has been set fairly high for Whiteside given his play in training camp and the first preseason game. However, he came back to Earth against the Commanders. Whiteside allowed the most receiving yards of all Lions defensive backs with 69 yards on three receptions. While 55 of those yards came on a deep shot to Nick Nash, those are 55 yards you hate to allow. Nash is far from a burner either (a 40-yard time of 4.57 seconds), but he simply outran Whiteside down the sideline. Another of Whiteside’s allowed catches came on a juke courtesy of Van Jefferson—Whiteside got bit with his hips facing outside while Jefferson cut inside for an easy catch. That being said, he did recover well to limit the catch to just a 4-yard gain. The main reason why I’m listing Whiteside here is not necessarily his performance, but because of the roster implications. While I have been impressed with Whiteside prior to this game, I still think the team values Ennis Rakestraw more—they drafted him early for a reason and likely still believe in his potential. If Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph start the season on the active 53-man roster, the secondary suddenly becomes very crowded. D.J. Reed, Rock Ya-Sin, Keith Abney, and Christian Izien are locks. Chuck Clark, Thomas Harper, and Avonte Maddox should be locks. Khalil Dorsey is an elite special teamer on a team without other reliable gunners. That is already 11 defensive backs to keep. That leaves Whiteside competing with Roger McCreary for a roster spot, a player who has quietly had a fantastic preseason (currently leading the defense in PFF grade). Whiteside is almost exclusively an outside cornerback, further limiting his value. I still think that Whiteside deserves a roster spot, but he might simply be a victim of the numbers game—he needs to be great, not just good to overcome the odds. Is that fair? Not really, but that is the nature of this roster. Colby Sorsdal, OL The book is all but closed on Sorsdal. Whether at guard or tackle, his performance on the field is simply not cutting it. Sorsdal got early looks at right tackle on Saturday, but after allowing a sack midway through the second quarter, he was pulled in favor of Miles Frazier. He would return later in the second half when more reserves were brought in, but his struggles persisted. In particular, he gave up a pressure that forced Joshua Dobbs into a slight overthrow of Tay Martin for what could have been a significant gain—Martin nearly had it, but with a split second more time, Dobbs would not have had to rush the throw. Given that the Lions are fairly set at tackle with Penei Sewell, Blake Miller, Larry Borom, and Miles Frazier, there is not much room for Sorsdal even if he was performing well. As for reserve spots on the roster, he has not even outperformed players like Devin Cochran, Mason Miller, Melvin Priestly. Not only is he unlikely to make the roster, he might not even make the practice squad. Dominic Lovett, WR Another stock down performance for Lovett, although this time for different reasons. Whereas he struggled with hands in the first preseason game (dropping two passes and muffing a punt), the red flag in this game was his lack of usage in general. Earlier in the week, special teams coordinator said that the punt return job was largely down to Greg Dortch and Tom Kennedy . That decision erases one avenue for Lovett to make the team, but he is failing to stand out in any other capacity. A week after leading the team in targets, Lovett had just two (out of 25 pass attempts) against the Commanders. His snap count plummeted from 39 last week to 14 this week, none of which came on special teams—no punt returns, no kick returns, no coverage. Most of his snaps came in the fourth quarter, well after players like Tay…

title: Discussion: What was the most promising part of the Lions’ win over the Commanders?
summary: The Detroit Lions defeated the Washington Commanders 17-13 on Saturday afternoon in their second preseason game of 2026. Obviously, the final score of the game matters little, but there were certainly developments during the game that were positive and negative. We’ll cover plenty of both over the next few days as we break down the […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - AUGUST 22: Jayden Daniels #5 of the Washington Commanders is sacked by DJ Wonnum #98 of the Detroit Lions during the first half at Ford Field on August 22, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions defeated the Washington Commanders 17-13 on Saturday afternoon in their second preseason game of 2026. Obviously, the final score of the game matters little, but there were certainly developments during the game that were positive and negative. We’ll cover plenty of both over the next few days as we break down the film, advanced statistics, and individual plays, but for now, let’s talk about the big-picture positives. Today’s Question of the Day is: What was the most promising thing about the Lions’ win over the Commanders? My answer: It has to be the continued strong play of the defensive line. On Saturday, the Lions saw a ton of great play from their big guys on defense. Derrick Moore provided a sack in his first NFL action. Rookie Skyler Gill-Howard was a total menace as a pass rusher throughout the game. I thought it was a promising game from Levi Onwuzurike, Tyler Lacy, and although his chances were limited to the very end of the game, Eric O’Neill looked disruptive again. And starter DJ Wonnum kicked things off with a solid performance, including a sack. In total, the Commanders managed just 35 rushing yards on 17 carries, were sacked two times, and endured six quarterback hits from six different players. Now, all of this needs to come with a pretty big caveat. No team in the NFL has good reserve offensive linemen. There is no resource more scarce in the NFL than good offensive linemen, so we should not overreact to how productive the Lions’ defensive front was. Just consider the opposite situation. Detroit is obviously going through some similar struggles with their own offensive line depth, and the Commanders put up five sacks on them. Defensive lines tend to look better in the preseason. Still, it’s hard not to be encouraged by Moore, who is just scratching the surface of what he’s capable now that the second-round pick is finally getting some reps following his groin injury. Gill-Howard is continuing to stack days and play against better competition both in practice and in games. And legit starters like Lacy, Wonnum, and Onwuzurike (in a subpackage role) are playing well, too. These are players that Detroit is going to rely upon at some point this year, and we haven’t even seen the Lions unleash Alim McNeill or Aidan Hutchinson yet. What were you most encouraged by from Saturday’s preseason game against the Commanders? Share your thoughts in the comment section. Join the conversation! title: Packers Discussion: How many Green Bay players are roster locks?
summary: It’s a little bit of a dead period in camp, where we can finally all catch our breath after Friday’s preseason game against the Denver Broncos. Why not embrace debate? How many players do you think have a roster spot locked in going into the preseason finale against the Arizona Cardinals, where the backups should […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - AUGUST 13: Tyrod Taylor #6 of the Green Bay Packers looks to pass during the second quarter against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Acrisure Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Joe Sargent/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s a little bit of a dead period in camp, where we can finally all catch our breath after Friday’s preseason game against the Denver Broncos. Why not embrace debate? How many players do you think have a roster spot locked in going into the preseason finale against the Arizona Cardinals, where the backups should be getting an extended look — as head coach Matt LaFleur stated last week that the starters will be getting reps in joint practice but will sit out the game? I’m probably a little more firm on my roster than most. Based on what I’ve seen on social media and the comment section here, I think fewer spots are up for grabs than the average fan. I’m sure I’ll have to eat crow on at least one of these locks, but this is truly how I feel about the roster going into the final week of the preseason. I am going to throw this disclaimer, though: This is assuming that players are healthy and they aren’t traded. If we ship a cornerback out or move on from an expiring contract, like defensive lineman Karl Brooks, I don’t really see that differently than them being rosterable in this exercise. With that being said, here’s my stab at who the roster locks are right now: Quarterback Jordan Love I don’t think we’re even at the point where the Packers will call Tyrod Taylor versus Kyle McCord a competition at this point, but it’s worth noting that Taylor has not played well in the preseason, while McCord, despite limited tools, has performed significantly better through two games. We opened up a thread earlier this weekend for your thoughts on the subject . Maybe Green Bay’s QB2 for the 2026 regular season is on another team right now. Either way, I’ve officially moved off my stance that Taylor is a roster lock after his performance against the Broncos. Running Back Josh Jacobs MarShawn Lloyd Chris Brooks Barring a suspension or an injury, I think it’s going to be difficult for Green Bay to keep RB4 Pierre Strong Jr., but I do think he will be a priority signing for them on the practice squad. I had Strong making the practice squad in our latest 53-man roster projection . Receiver Christian Watson Matthew Golden Jayden Reed Savion Williams Bo Melton Skyy Moore Usually I stay away from nailing down six receivers making the roster, but this year is a little different. Unlike in the past, where receivers have moved around all over, it seems like this year’s Packers have defined roles for pass-catchers, including their direct backups. Matthew Golden is the X, and his backup is Bo Melton. Christian Watson is the Z, and his backup is Savion Williams. Jayden Reed is the slot, and his backup is Skyy Moore. On top of that, Williams (lead blocker on punt returns, punt gunner on punt and returner on kickoff), Melton (jammer on punt returns and gunner on punt) and Moore (returner on both punts and kicks) are also in line for significant special teams snaps. I wouldn’t call J. Michael Sturdivant a “roster lock” at this point, but I will say he’s my guess for the next man up at the position. He’s one spot lower than Isaiah Neyor in the pass-catching pecking order right now, but they have him training on various special teams roles (similar to Williams), which really helps out if there’s ever an injury at receiver or defensive back. The same cannot be said of Neyor, who is more of a true receiver than a special teams contributor. Sturdivant’s special teams contributions go back to college, where he was the lead blocker on Florida’s kickoff team. It’s worth mentioning here, too, that Williams and Sturdivant both dropped out of the game on Friday with injuries. Williams played two plays before injuring his ankle, and Sturdivant was evaluated for a concussion. We don’t know anything about their injuries other than that, but should learn more on Monday in LaFleur’s pre-practice press conference. LaFleur didn’t speak to the media on Saturday, as he subbed in offensive assistants and special teams coordinator Cam Achord for interviews , after LaFleur was slated for an appearance. Tight End Tucker Kraft Josh Whyle Tight end was a position where the Packers were already thin, and then Luke Musgrave injured his neck and has spent all of camp on the physically unable to perform list. The next man up is Drake Dabney, but I’m not sure Green Bay even needs to keep him on their initial 53-man roster to play him in Week 1. I could also see the team claiming a player at the position at cutdowns. Offensive Line Zach Bako-Bewele Jordan Morgan Sean Rhyan Aaron Banks Anthony Belton Jacob Monk Jager Burton John Williams Darian Kinnard Maybe I’m naive, but I still think it’s going to be hard for the team to get rid of Darian Kinnard, who is technically the 10th offensive lineman in the pecking order right now, after he was their top sub in 2025. They spent a pick on him last summer, gave him a new contract and paid him $1 million in guarantees. If the team keeps 10 offensive linemen, the 10th will probably be guard/center Donovan Jennings, but the team already has so many guard/center bodies that I’m not sure if he’ll 100 percent make the team. Defensive Line Devonte Wyatt Karl Brooks Javon Hargrave Warren Brinson Chris McClellan This is sort of self-explanatory, as the real competition in the defensive line room right now is for the sixth spot. Currently, Nazir Stackhouse, Anthony Campbell and Jonathan Ford are all making their cases for what will probably be the last spot on the team — unless Karl Brooks (contract year) gets traded or there’s an injury. I go back and forth between Campbell and Ford making the team, so Week 3 of the preseason will be a big deal there. Edge Defender Lukas Van Ness Barryn Sorrell Brenton Cox Jr. Collin Oliver Dani Dennis-Sutton With Micah Parsons starting the year on the PUP list, this one seems like a layup. The bigger question with his position, from a numbers standpoint, is if the team will cut one of Brenton Cox Jr. (one year remaining on his contract) or Collin Oliver (three years remaining on his contract) once Parsons returns. Off-Ball Linebacker Zaire Franklin Edgerrin Cooper Isaiah McDuffie Ty’Ron Hopper Nick Niemann This is another easy one. This is the same group that the team had in 2025, but instead of Quay Walker playing the Mike, it’s Zaire Franklin. Nick Niemann is a core special teams player, which is why he’s likely to make the 53-man roster. Niemann played 16.3 special teams snaps per game last year, which, if he had stayed healthy for 17 games, would have ranked second on the team behind only special teams captain Isaiah McDuffie. Niemann is going to help the Packers cover their butts, as Zayne Anderson (now a Miami Dolphin) and Arron Mosby (likely a practice squadder) probably won’t be on Green Bay’s 53-man roster in Week 1. They were two of the five most-played special teamers on the 2025 team. Outside Cornerback Keisean Nixon Carrington Valentine Brandon Cisse Benjamin St-Juste I think the Packers will probably keep a fifth outside cornerback, but that’s still a little up in the air right now. Domani Jackson, a rookie sixth-round pick, just returned to practice last week after undergoing an offseason surgery to his core. In his preseason debut, he was a spot behind Jaylin Simpson, who was on the team’s practice squad for most of 2025, in the pecking order. Simpson had a better performance against the Broncos, but he put up some bad film in Week 1 against the Steelers. Safety/Slot Xavier McKinney Evan Williams Javon Bullard Kitan Oladapo Kamal Hadden I’m going to combine the safety and slot positions here, since they have a lot of overlap. Kamal Hadden was the team’s preferred slot defender after returning to the field from his season-ending ankle injury, and he looked a lot…

title: Packers Film Room, Preseason Week 2: Jordan Love
summary: Last week, we looked at Green Bay Packers quarterback Jordan Love’s 5 dropbacks in the opening preseason game. We’re doing the same thing with this week’s game against the Denver Broncos. Love and the first-team offense only got one drive, but it was a long one: a 12-play, 63-yard drive that took 6 minutes & […]
full_text: DENVER, COLORADO - AUGUST 21: Jordan Love #10 of the Green Bay Packers motions before a play in the first quarter of a preseason game against the Denver Broncos at Empower Field at Mile High on August 21, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Tyler Schank/Clarkson Creative/Getty Images) | Getty Images Last week, we looked at Green Bay Packers quarterback Jordan Love’s 5 dropbacks in the opening preseason game. We’re doing the same thing with this week’s game against the Denver Broncos. Love and the first-team offense only got one drive, but it was a long one: a 12-play, 63-yard drive that took 6 minutes & 35 seconds and was capped with a TD pass. On that drive, Love had 7 dropbacks. He went 5/7 for 56 yards and 1 TD. Let’s dig in. Dropback 1: 1st & 10, 14:55 remaining in the 1st quarter Last week, the Packers opened with a quick-out to Christian Watson, and the timing was slightly off. This week they opened with a play-action deep-out to Watson. It’s a perfectly good throw, but Riley Moss does a good job of reading Watson’s route and getting his hands on the ball to break it up. Between you, me, and the fencepost, Watson could probably do a better job of attacking this pass and protecting it from Moss, but it is a nice play by Moss to drive on this ball. They went with a mirrored look here (both sides of the field running the same route/concept). This is something we haven’t really seen much out of the Packers since Aaron Rodgers was playing QB. The idea behind mirrored concepts is to let the QB read the defense pre-snap and immediately post-snap and allow him to decide which side of the field to throw to based on that. Since it’s the same concept, it becomes an if-this-then-that read. “Do I like the way the defense is presenting more on the left or the right?” It can sometimes be a simplified version of offense, but it’s also an interesting idea to mix in a little more if you trust your QB. In a world where defenses are getting more complex every year and offenses have begun utilizing full-field reads more, mirrored concepts is a way to give the QB full control while also allowing him to get the ball out quickly on a favorable match-up. I don’t know if this is something that the Packers are using in the preseason simply because it gives less away or if it’s something they’re going to be using more as part of their offense this year. Either way, it’s something to keep an eye on over the first couple weeks of the season. Dropback 2: 2nd & 10, 14:49 remaining in the 1st quarter Dragon (slant/flat) out of a split backfield look and Love with an absolute laser. Watson is running a slant from the outside with Skyy Moore running a flat route from the backfield. We get a man coverage tell pre-snap, so this looks like a pretty easy read. If they’re truly in man, Moore will be covered by a linebacker, so Love would just wait for the LB to clear the window then throw to Watson. The Broncos mix things up a bit, with the LB holding in place to watch Love while the safety takes Moore out of the backfield. That still leaves a window for Love, but one that he has to keep open. He starts by looking down the middle of the field, then works back to Watson. Watson gets inside leverage on Pat Surtain II, but the LB over Moore is still sitting in the middle of the field. Love puts some serious mustard on this ball, zipping it past the LB waiting in the middle of the field. Or maybe it’s sauerkraut. Whatever you prefer, I guess. This was ruled a fumble on the field, but Watson was ruled down on replay. Dropback 3: 3rd & 1, 12:55 remaining in the 1st quarter Packers go with an old favorite, PA Boot. This one is slightly different in that it’s a frontside boot. Watson is running the Sail route, Matthew Golden is on the crosser and Josh Whyle is on the flat. Typically the Packers will run this with Love turning his back and booting the other way, so this frontside boot is slightly rarer, but it’s still something you’ll see them run quite a few times in the regular season. Nothing too exotic here. Nick Bonitto stays home and is baring down on Love, so Love dirts it. Dropback 4: 4th & 1, 12:51 remaining in the 1st quarter The Packers go for it on the very next play. Once again, they go with a variant of PA Boot. It’s kind of a PA Boot/High Cross mix, with Watson running a deep crossing route over Golden. The pocket is slightly moving, but not a true bootleg. It looks like they’re trying to play this off as PA Boot, with Love hoping to hit Watson in the other direction for a big gain. Get the defense leaning and hit them with a big play. On a true PA Boot, you typically leave the End Man On the Line (EMOL) unblocked, with the concept itself taking him out of the play. With this play not calling for a true bootleg, Chris Brooks is set to block the EMOL, but he isn’t able to stay in front, leaving Jonathan Cooper with a run right in Love’s face. With Whyle working as the flat control, there’s a window open for Golden on the crosser, so Love takes a half-step back, lowers his arm angle, and hits Golden. Good read by Love and a really nice adjustment. He talked in the offseason about getting better on his footwork in the pocket. I think this is still something he does last year, but that slight step-back-and-throw is nice to see. I also love the placement on this. Typically the route from Golden stays fairly flat across the field, but the throw from Love leads Golden upfield, away from the defender closing from underneath. Dropback 5: 1st & 10, 12:12 remaining in the 1st quarter Another PA Boot. Man, they really don’t like showing a ton, huh? I get it. I like it. Love hits Drake Dabney in the flat. Next. Dropback 6: 1st & 10, 9:43 remaining in the 1st quarter PA Boot. Watson on the slide. Slightly different formation from the last time and the flat route comes from a different place. In the last play, Dabney has a block-and-release off the same side as the flat. This time, Watson releases to the flat under the formation. This can really help hammer home the whole “illusion of complexity” thing. Dropback 7: 3rd & 1, 8:30 remaining in the 1st quarter In the red zone in Nub formation (three receivers to one side of the formation, with the other side of the formation featuring an in-line TE). The Packers are running a Smash variant (with an underneath rub) on the right side. On the left side, Whyle is running a corner route, and MarShawn Lloyd is running an option route from the backfield. Love does a nice job of working back to the left and finding Lloyd in the middle of the field, and Lloyd does the rest. Nice route from Lloyd. He pushes out, keeping inside leverage on the defender. When he cuts back to the inside, he has a nice patch of green grass to work in. I know it’s only preseason, but it was awesome to see Lloyd get this TD. After everything he has been through over the last couple of years, I bet he felt amazing being able to get into the end zone here. Let’s hope we see it even more during the regular season. This was a really nice showing from Love and the starting offense. Something notable here is how they ran the offense. Yes, they kept it fairly simple, but it was primarily through moving pockets. You can read that a couple different ways. The first reading is that the Packers were keeping this simple and leaning on some of their core passing concept. Don’t give anything away. Keep it vanilla, etc. The other reading goes hand-in-hand with some of the changes on the offensive line. It hasn’t been any secret that the Packers have been looking to get bigger on the offensive line over the last few years, as a way to lean more into the power running game. With Jager Burton and Jacob Monk getting time at guard this preseason, they have shown a smaller look. Smaller guards would support a return to Wide Zone being a bigger part of this offense. And if Wide Zone is a bigger part of this offense, that pocket movement – PA Boot, half-boots, etc. – would naturally be a bigger…
author: Dusty Evely

title: Breaking down Riley Leonard’s performance vs the Falcons
summary: It was Riley Leonard’s chance to play with the 2’s and it was nothing to write home about. Below are many of throws and plays from his performance against the Falcons. Scramble 1 This is a nice scramble and run from Leonard. His receivers were clearly covered throughout the entire play and he picked up […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - AUGUST 22: Riley Leonard #15 of the Indianapolis Colts looks to pass during the first quarter of the preseason game against the Atlanta Falcons at Lucas Oil Stadium on August 22, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Chris Carter/Getty Images) | Getty Images It was Riley Leonard’s chance to play with the 2’s and it was nothing to write home about. Below are many of throws and plays from his performance against the Falcons. Scramble 1 Leonard picks up the first but this one is coming back due to a hold on Dalton Tucker #Colts #ForTheShoe #Falcons #ATLvsIND pic.twitter.com/nYUbUCoy76 — Chris Shepherd (@NFLscheme) August 22, 2026 This is a nice scramble and run from Leonard. His receivers were clearly covered throughout the entire play and he picked up the first down with his legs and smartly went out of bounds. Throw 1 Big completion to Coleman Owen. #Colts #ForTheShoe #Falcons #ATLvsIND pic.twitter.com/YF66Jhtz9F — Chris Shepherd (@NFLscheme) August 22, 2026 This is a longer developing route with a post/corner pick down the field. The protection was nice here, giving Leonard enough time in the pocket to scan and make a nice throw to Owen who was wide open after the nice play design. Throw 2 Deon Burks with a catch short of the sticks. #Colts #ForTheShoe #Falcons #ATLvsIND pic.twitter.com/R2a3PVXYii — Chris Shepherd (@NFLscheme) August 22, 2026 The protection can be partially blamed on this one. It appeared that a dig route was going to open up perfectly over the middle but Leonard had to rush the throw underneath to Burks who was stopped short of the sticks. It’s not a bad decision or throw considering the circumstances surrounding the play. Throw 3 PI for a first down. Raylen Sharpe the target. #Colts #ForTheShoe #Falcons #ATLvsIND pic.twitter.com/w6vLQzClUI — Chris Shepherd (@NFLscheme) August 22, 2026 The out underneath was probably the better decision but Leonard wanted to throw one up for the 1on1 and he was rewarded with a pass interference that got them that yardage. I believe if both scenarios (throw the out or take the 1on1 shot) were played out 10 times, the throw to the out is likely the more successful one, but the 1on1 shot was the better one on this play. Throw 4 Big completion for Deon Burks for a first down. Coming back due to an illegal hands to the face on Josh Kreutz. #Colts #ForTheShoe #Falcons #ATLvsIND pic.twitter.com/fhljWVpBsW — Chris Shepherd (@NFLscheme) August 22, 2026 This is a very nice throw in the pocket and especially impressive as it came on 3rd down. He threaded the needle beautifully on it. Throw 5 Leonard dirts this ball on 3rd down. #Colts #ForTheShoe #Falcons #ATLvsIND pic.twitter.com/NTfwDoU4jc — Chris Shepherd (@NFLscheme) August 22, 2026 This is a flat out miss that simply can’t happen. He doesn’t step into his throw properly and it could be because he was thrown off by the timing. Nevertheless, a bad miss that leads to a punt deep in their own zone. Throw 6 Nice catch from 80 #Colts #ForTheShoe #Falcons #ATLvsIND pic.twitter.com/IqiStxEeUu — Chris Shepherd (@NFLscheme) August 22, 2026 While the throw was a slight floater, it was very well placed and well timed. He threw that in a spot where only Burks can make the catch. Throw 7 Another grab for Burks. #Colts #ForTheShoe #Falcons #ATLvsIND pic.twitter.com/H0QcL8kKtB — Chris Shepherd (@NFLscheme) August 22, 2026 This was the right read and a bit unfortunate that Burks just got caught before the sideline. Not much Leonard could do… holding on to it longer makes the throw more difficult, especially to a receiver moving away from him. Throwing it too early and the defense has more time to adjust, react and make a play on Burks before he gets out of bounds. Overall Recap While this breakdown is somewhat incomplete due to the lack of available clips from Leonard’s game, I came away thinking there were more positives than negatives and plenty to be encouraged about. This QB2 battle is nowhere near over. Richardson had two fantastic drives last week against the Patriots with the 2s, and Leonard had several positive plays and throws with the 2s this week. People will want to crown Richardson as the QB2 after his strong couple of drives last week, but objective fans and analysts know this battle is far from over. While Richardson moved the ball well on drives that led to points, Leonard made some big throws on third down and did not turn the ball over. The Richardson situation over the past few years has made many fans overly emotional, and once you take off the Florida Gators-colored glasses, you see a very tight race that is not close to over. Next week’s game will be the final battle before the team is forced to make a decision. While both quarterbacks showed some positive signs in their games with the 2s, the harsh reality is that neither looks ready for regular-season NFL action. If the Colts were forced to play either backup right now, they would be in serious trouble.

title: 6 winners and 5 losers from the Chiefs’ second preseason game
summary: Saturday’s preseason matchup between the Kansas City Chiefs and Tampa Bay Buccaneers actually had a few plays with the excitement of a regular-season game: a record-breaking field goal, some real pass rush, and a run game. The ending was a letdown, but there were plenty of standout players to discuss: 6 Winners Defensive end Felix Anudike-Uzomah: The biggest play of […]
full_text: Aug 22, 2026; Tampa, Florida, USA; Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Justin Fields (6) throws against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers during the first half at Raymond James Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Kim Klement Neitzel-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Saturday’s preseason matchup between the Kansas City Chiefs and Tampa Bay Buccaneers actually had a few plays with the excitement of a regular-season game: a record-breaking field goal, some real pass rush, and a run game. The ending was a letdown, but there were plenty of standout players to discuss: 6 Winners Defensive end Felix Anudike-Uzomah: The biggest play of the game was FAU crushing the Tampa Bay QB for his (and the Chiefs defense’s) first sack of the preseason. Perhaps the former first-round pick is developing after all? If he can be a part of the rotation and play like he consistently did on Saturday, Felix can change the trajectory of his career. Defensive end R Mason Thomas and Cornerback Mansoor Delane: Do the Chiefs finally have speed on defense? From what we saw out of Delane in his NFL debut, he’s got the acceleration, instincts, and lack of fear to be a factor in the run game. Given his ability in coverage, he looks like a complete corner. The R Mason Thomas hype just keeps building as he showed his explosive ability on the edge and nearly had a pick-six against the Bucs. Adding these two to the young defense feels like it has sped up the entire unit– which was sorely needed. Wide receiver Jalen Royals: He needed to make himself visible. Jalen Royals certainly did that, leading the Chiefs with 51 yards receiving. Known as a run-after-the-catch guy, it’s critical for Royals to be a reliable pass catcher to see the field on offense. On Saturday, he caught all six of his targets. It was a promising performance to build upon. Wide receiver Cyrus Allen and running back Brashard Smith: The new-look Chiefs offense is going to need some role players to throw as a change-up. Allen and Smith appear to be the most likely candidates, especially after watching them on Saturday. Allen got some of the gadget plays previously belonging to the Mecole Hardmans of the world. Smith saw plenty of use as a runner and receiver, as coaches recently praised his improvement in pass protection. Both guys got reps returning punts, which could signal the team is looking for ways to save a roster spot and let these guys serve a variety of roles. 5 Losers Note: Applying the labels “losers” is not intended to be a judgment on the talent or character of any of these players. It’s just a simple way to grade their performance in a single game. No disrespect should be inferred. Offensive Lineman Kahlil Benson: The Chiefs were without two of their best offensive linemen on Saturday, while Josh Simmons and Trey Smith rehabbed (hopefully minor) injuries. The results weren’t exactly confidence-inspiring. The rookie took a step back in his quest to win a starting job. He struggled in pass protection, bullied by NFL Draft darling Rueben Bain Jr. Some experts commented that Benson might just be a guard — though I’d argue it’s too early to give up on the kid. Special Teams Coordinator Dave Toub: When your kicker nails a 69-yard field goal, it should be a day to praise the special teams units. But there were penalties on nearly every return (and not much yardage on the plus side). Then, Harrison Butker missed an extra point and a field goal that would change the outcome of the game. Toub appears to be trying out a number of returners, likely looking at roster cuts. But the execution is lacking across the board, indicating a broader coaching issue. Cornerback Kristian Fulton: The once promising defensive back has become the most discussed potential cap casualty on the team. The pattern of developing young cornerbacks from the draft continues as the rookies seem to be outplaying the veteran. Defensive end Ethan Hurkett: The Iowa Hawkeye product stood out in the wrong ways late in Saturday’s game. I don’t really have stats or deep analysis to back this up; he just didn’t look like he belonged on an NFL roster. I hope he proves me wrong. Quarterback Justin Fields: I really hope the Chiefs use Fields in designed running situations.
author: Matt Stagner

title: Chiefs Preseason Week 2 snap count analysis: Jalen Royals leads offense
summary: Welcome back to Arrowhead Pride’s weekly snap-count analysis! During the preseason, we will shorten the analysis as it is difficult to make definitive statements based on the raw snap-count data. Still, let’s see what we can figure out about the Kansas City Chiefs when taking a closer look at playing time during the 16-15 loss […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - JUNE 09: Jalen Royals #11 of the Kansas City Chiefs lines up out wide during mandatory minicamp at The University of Kansas Hospital Arrowhead Training Complex on June 09, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Aaron M. Sprecher/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome back to Arrowhead Pride’s weekly snap-count analysis! During the preseason, we will shorten the analysis as it is difficult to make definitive statements based on the raw snap-count data. Still, let’s see what we can figure out about the Kansas City Chiefs when taking a closer look at playing time during the 16-15 loss at the hands of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Saturday. Starters (offensive): LT Jaylon Moore, LG Kingsley Suamataia, C Creed Humphrey, RG Mike Caliendo, RT Kahlil Benson, QB Justin Fields, WR Tyquan Thornton, WR Jalen Royals, WR Cyrus Allen, RB Kenneth Walker, TE Travis Kelce Starters (defensive): DE George Karlaftis, DT Chris Jones, DT Khyiris Tonga, DE Felix Anudike-Uzomah, LB Nick Bolton, LB Jeffrey Bassa, S Christian Roland-Wallace, CB Nohl Williams, CB Mansoor Delane, S Jaden Hicks, S Xavier Nwankpa Did not play: QB Patrick Mahomes, WR Rashee Rice (Knee), WR Jimmy Holiday, RG Trey Smith (Hip), LT Josh Simmons (Back), S Chamarri Conner, LB Drue Tranquill (Back spasms), LB Jack Cochrane (Knee), CB L’Jarius Sneed (Knee), DE Ashton Gillotte (Hamstring), S Alohi Gilman (Low-back spasms), WR Jeff Weimer, WR Jeff Caldwell (Hyperextended knee), OT Kellen Diesch, TE Mason Pline, DT Omarr Norman-Lott (PUP) The big takeaway Second-year wide receiver Jalen Royals led all wideouts in snaps on offense (36). He also played five snaps on special teams. He led the entire offense in skill-position production, catching all six of his targets and gaining 51 yards. Jalen Royals didn't look easy to bring down with the ball in his hands. Forced 5 missed tackles over his 6 catches (PFF) On his 17-yard gain, you like seeing him come back to the ball to and be strong at the catch point too! pic.twitter.com/O11LQAN199 — Ron Kopp Jr (@RonOnChiefs) August 23, 2026 What stood out the most over Royals’ playing time was his play strength after the ball gets in his hands. According to Pro Football Focus , Royals forced five missed tackles over the six times he caught a pass. However, he also came back to the ball and secured it with strength on the 17-yard gain, courtesy of a nice play by rookie quarterback Garrett Nussmeier. It was a strong performance for a player who needed to showcase more of his talents in live action. The Offensive takeaway After rookie offensive lineman Kahlil Benson took just six snaps with the starting offensive line at right guard in the preseason opener, Benson got an extended stretch of playing time at right tackle on Saturday night. He was on the field for 35 snaps, all of them on the right edge of the line. The Chiefs needed to give Benson the live-action look against the Tampa Bay starting defensive front. It exposed Benson on two specific snaps, although those were the only two pressures he allowed over 25 pass-blocking opportunities (PFF). The lingering question from this game about Benson will be where he lines up in the preseason finale. If right guard Trey Smith can return to the lineup, he needs to be playing alongside the Week 1 starter. The Defensive takeaway Rookie, second-round edge rusher R Mason Thomas was not among the first out on the field for the Chiefs’ starting defense, but he was a factor for the first-team unit. On an early third-and-11, Thomas flew up the field with his head and hands up, batting down a pass that was nearly lateral and staying with it through the whistle. It was just one play that showed off his pass-rushing prowess, but there were a number of chances for Thomas to rush the passer. In fact, all 15 of Thomas’ defensive snaps in Tampa were against a pass play, and he did not drop into coverage on any of those reps. PFF marked Thomas with four pressures over the 15 opportunities, including a quarterback hit. Editor’s Note : Arrowhead Pride will present charts with updated snap-count data in this weekly post during the regular season.
author: Ron Kopp Jr.

title: Preseason Week 2 notes for Chiefs’ offense, defense and special teams
summary: The Kansas City Chiefs played a preseason game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Saturday night. Many players were out for both teams, so there’s not too much you can take away from this game. Still, important things happen in the preseason that translate to the regular season. Here are three things I took away […]
full_text: TAMPA, FLORIDA - AUGUST 22: Khalil Benson #70 of the Kansas City Chiefs blocks Rueben Bain #3 of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers during the first half of a preseason game at Raymond James Stadium on August 22, 2026 in Tampa, Florida. (Photo by Mike Carlson/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Kansas City Chiefs played a preseason game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Saturday night. Many players were out for both teams, so there’s not too much you can take away from this game. Still, important things happen in the preseason that translate to the regular season. Here are three things I took away from the game that I feel matter in the regular season. Offense Tackle options behind Josh Simmons are concerning The most essential player on the Chiefs is quarterback Patrick Mahomes. After watching last night’s preseason game, it’s hard to come to any other conclusion than left tackle Josh Simmons being the second-most essential Chief this year. Simmons didn’t play in this game with a back injury. Veteran Jaylon Moore was the starting left tackle with Khalil Benson playing right tackle. When Moore went to the bench in the second quarter, Esa Pole took over at left tackle. All three tackles looked poor in this game. Moore was giving up the corner consistently. He struggled getting out of his stance to cut off the corner, which was a problem for him last year. Benson has been getting first-team reps with the offense throughout training camp. Benson has shown good signs as a run blocker. He’s good on the backside of zone runs where he works on the backside defensive tackle and opens a cutback lane. He’s even shown some ability to pull and move in space. Anthony Nelson bringing the pressure on defense 💪 Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/XXDZBHqHPu — NFL (@NFL) August 23, 2026 However, in pass protection, Benson doesn’t look ready to play in the NFL. Bain with a sick hump move. Sheesh! pic.twitter.com/err5hv3PH2 — Billy M (@BillyM_91) August 22, 2026 He’s struggled to get out of his stance and meet pass rushers at the top of the arc. He’s had to open his hips too far to try and cut off the corner, which led to Buccaneers defensive end Reuben Bain using that against him by going inside on a hump move and nearly getting a sack. When Pole came in for Moore, things got worse. Pole was getting plenty of reps going one-on-one with Buccaneers reserve pass rusher David Walker, and Walker was feasting on that matchup. Walker was winning in every way, constantly getting Pole off balance. He was easily getting around the corner before Pole could wash him out. David Walker is easily the best player on the field right now The Chiefs can’t stop his pass rush bag pic.twitter.com/a8INsLoDLF — NFL Draft Files (@NFL_DF) August 23, 2026 Walker used an inside spin move in this game that nearly resulted in a sack. Pole had chip help from rookie running back Emmett Johnson, so all he needed to do was protect his inside shoulder, and he wasn’t able to do that. David Walker showed plenty of juice off the edge. Very close to having 3 sacks pic.twitter.com/1CZ1Yixzvs — Billy M (@BillyM_91) August 23, 2026 When Simmons plays, the Chiefs’ lack of tackle depth will be less glaring. I’m terrified of the options at right tackle right now, but the other four offensive linemen are so good that it will help. The offense can use chips and add extra bodies to help any right tackle since Simmons doesn’t need any help. However, if Simmons gets hurt at all, the Chiefs might be screwed offensively. The unit wouldn’t be able to pass protect at all. The coaching staff couldn’t call any downfield dropbacks. The play calling would have to keep two chips in at all times, which limits you to three downfield receivers. Mahomes might not move as much this year, making tackle play even more important. Suffice to say, the team cannot lose Simmons for any extended period this year. Defense Edge rush has a different level of explosiveness, but Peter Woods has been concerningly quiet On the flip side, there are things to be encouraged about with the defensive line, particularly at defensive end. To start, former first-round pick Felix Anudike-Uzomah looked very good in this game. Anudike-Uzomah showed a different level of explosiveness and first step in this preseason game. Anudike-Uzomah’s get-off has been poor throughout his career, so it was staggering to see how well he got off the ball and around the corner in this game. FAU said “Here comes the BOOM” 💥 pic.twitter.com/Z4gStRNXbO — Arrowhead Pride (@ArrowheadPride) August 23, 2026 Now, Anudike-Uzomah was going up against backup tackles, so he still needs to prove he can do that to starting tackles. With that being said, he has never looked this athletic even in preseason. There’s reason to believe he could give the Chiefs some pass-rush presence this year. R Mason Thomas SHEESH 🔥 🎥 via @ClayWendler pic.twitter.com/bbLZlrLmY2 — SleeperChiefs (@SleeperChiefsKC) August 23, 2026 The Chiefs’ second-round rookie, R Mason Thomas, had nice flashes in this game after a few in preseason Week 1. It’s very clear that Thomas’s quickness is legit and something this team needed. His get-off and burst can get him quick wins in a way no other recent defensive end has had. Thomas has the get-off to blow up plays before they even happen. Now, similar to Anudike-Uzomah, we’ll need to see Thomas do it against starting tackles that are more prepared for his speed. One thing Thomas does need to improve is his balance and bend. He does a good job getting to the top of the arc, but he needs to work on his balance to turn that tight corner. He’s still struggling to maintain his speed at that point. If he can improve that, he could be a devastating speed rusher. On the negative side, I haven’t been impressed with rookie defensive tackle Peter Woods through two preseason games. All the concerns I had about Woods at Clemson have shown up in these two games. Woods has lacked power in his hands, and he has struggled to get off blocks. He hasn’t been able to control blockers or use his hands to get off a punch of a guard. He’s often getting stuck on blocks and not creating any movement. Because Woods has short arms, he can’t easily knock around blockers with his hands and control the block. He needs to get significantly better at using hand quickness to beat guards to the punch. Woods needs to win at a faster rate, because once a guard gets his hands on him, he struggles to get off that block with his lack of length. Woods will still contribute as a run defender as a rookie, but I’m not banking on instant pass-rush production right now. Special teams How did Harrison Butker do that? Preseason football isn’t that entertaining, but Harrison Butker nailing a 69-yard kick before halftime was insane. That kick might’ve been good from 75 yards. Even if these games don’t count, that was one of the craziest things I’ve ever seen while watching football. My how times have changed. Kickers nowadays routinely make 50- and 60-yard field goals. In September of 1978, NBC's Marv Albert and Bob Trumpy were incredulous that the Seahawks' Efrén Herrera — a Pro Bowler and one of the best kickers of his era — connected on a 45-yarder. pic.twitter.com/Q2IVG6gDub — Kevin Gallagher (@KevG163) August 20, 2026 It’s amazing to see how good these kickers have gotten in 2026, considering these broadcasters from 1978 lost their minds over a “long-range” kick of 45 yards.
author: Nate Christensen

title: 5 things we learned from the Chiefs’ second preseason game of the season
summary: For a while, it looked like the Kansas City Chiefs might win a preseason game for the first time since 2023. The Chiefs were in control of the game on both offense and defense, and special teams looked like it had put together a special night. And then former Kansas Jayhawks quarterback Jalon Daniels came […]
full_text: TAMPA, FLORIDA - AUGUST 22: Harrison Butker #7 of the Kansas City Chiefs watches his field goal against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers during the first half of a preseason game at Raymond James Stadium on August 22, 2026 in Tampa, Florida. (Photo by Mike Carlson/Getty Images) | Getty Images For a while, it looked like the Kansas City Chiefs might win a preseason game for the first time since 2023. The Chiefs were in control of the game on both offense and defense, and special teams looked like it had put together a special night. And then former Kansas Jayhawks quarterback Jalon Daniels came into the game, and suddenly, the Tampa Bay Buccaneers offense had a spark. Still, with three minutes left to go in the game, Kansas City had a shot to kick the go-ahead field goal, but kicker Harrison Butker pushed it far right, costing the Chiefs an exhibition win. In the end, the Chiefs dropped this one on the road to the Buccaneers by a score of 16-15 . Thank God, it’s still the preseason and the results don’t matter, but we still learned five things from Saturday night: 1. Harrison Butker is still the human ying yang It was the best of Butker’s, it was the worst of Butker’s, it was the Butker of focus, it was the Butker of zoning out, it was the preseason of 69-yard field goals to end the half, it was the preseason of missed 43-yarders to lose the game, it was the Butker who gave hope, it was the Butker of despair, one moment we have faith we’re going to win the Super Bowl, the next we are terrified of missing the playoffs. One moment, he is a demigod, performing near-immortal feats with the grace and ease of Apollo’s arrows, and the next he looks like Edgar from “Men in Black.” In short, we never know which Harrison Butker we are going to get. 2. Right tackle might be a problem Hello darkness, my old friend. Here we are again, another season around the corner, and we have no idea how we are going to keep defenders from blowing around the right edge like they’re slingshotting around the sun in a stolen Klingon Bird-of-Prey. It didn’t matter who Andy Reid put in at offensive tackle on Saturday night. Jaylon Moore, Kahlil Benson, Esa Pole, etc. — they were all ineffective and at times downright horrible. It’s becoming more and more clear that Benson getting first-team reps is less about him being a diamond in the rough, and more about there being a lack of a better option. 3. FA-Who?!?! FAU, that’s who. Raise your hand if you did a double take in the first half when Chiefs edge rusher Felix Anudike-Uzomah came flying around the edge and obliterated Buccaneers quarterback Jake Browning? FAU said “Here comes the BOOM” 💥 pic.twitter.com/Z4gStRNXbO — Arrowhead Pride (@ArrowheadPride) August 23, 2026 For a guy who is fighting for his career, this is exactly the sort of thing we need to see out of Anudike-Uzomah. If the Chiefs can rely on this sort of play from the fourth-year pass rusher, the pass rush starts to look a little more daunting for opposing offenses. There is a world where Anudike-Uzomah and rookie R Mason Thomas are on the field at the same time, hunting quarterbacks like a pair of velociraptors. Throw George Karlaftis and Chris Jones in the mix, and suddenly you’re cooking with gas. 4. This is the Jalen Royals we’ve been waiting for Second-year wide receiver Jalen Royals caught all six of his targets in this game for a team high 51-yards in this game. Royals was a highly touted prospect, coming out of Utah State last season, but the hype never materialized in 2025. Up until Saturday night, it appeared to be more of the same. It’s not just that Royals caught all six of his targets; it’s that after the catch he looked dangerous and ran with a purpose once he had the ball in his hand. The Chiefs coaching staff has been waiting for a player to differentiate themselves from the pack and step up as quarterback Patrick Mahomes’ favorite new target. Perhaps this is the beginning of a new chapter for Royals, or perhaps none of this matters because it’s still just the preseason. 5. Masoor Delane is who we thought he was He didn’t play much in this game, but in the limited snaps he got, Delane looked like the blue-chip prospect he was in college. If Kansas City can lock down the boundary with a pair of young defensive backs, in Mansoor Delane and Nohl Williams, there is enough on tape that you can see the plan on defense starting to take shape. And if the defense can get after the opposing QB while locking down their receivers, then it could be a fun year on third downs in Arrowhead Stadium this season.
author: Rocky Magaña

title: Chiefs News: The rookies are flashing athleticism and speed on defense
summary: The latest The Kansas City Chiefs dropped to 0-2 in the preseason with a 16-15 loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Saturday evening. It was another exhibition loss — but it was another low-scoring affair. The Chiefs’ defense has performed well this preseason, especially on third down. Opponents have been kept out of the […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - AUGUST 15: Defensive end R. Mason Thomas #51 of the Kansas City Chiefs stands on the sidelines during the fourth quarter of an NFL preseason game against the Los Angeles Rams at Arrowhead Stadium on August 15, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by David Eulitt/Getty Images) | Getty Images The latest The Kansas City Chiefs dropped to 0-2 in the preseason with a 16-15 loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Saturday evening. It was another exhibition loss — but it was another low-scoring affair. The Chiefs’ defense has performed well this preseason, especially on third down. Opponents have been kept out of the end zone for the most part, and the rookies on defense have flashed their speed and athleticism. Five things that stood out about the Chiefs’ loss to the Bucs in NFL preseason | The Kansas City Star There were common themes— or purposes — with the initial wave of a defensive-filled draft class. Athleticism. And speed at the line of scrimmage. On back-to-back plays, they popped. Mansoor Delane, the first-round cornerback, derailed a wide receiver screen when he read the call from the jump and forced David Sills to cut inside for a 1-yard loss. A snap later, R Mason Thomas, the second-round edge, read another wide receiver screen and jumped in the lane to knock down a pass. Chiefs can’t hold halftime lead in 16-15 loss to Buccaneers | KMBC 9 The Chiefs took 9-0 halftime lead behind three Harrison Butker fields, including a 69-yarder, but Tampa Bay rallied. Kansas City’s defense, particularly through the first three quarters, did its job. Rookie Emmett Johnson scored Kansas City’s only touchdown of the game and lone touchdown of the preseason. Chiefs stock report: Rookies flash potential — again — in preseason loss to Bucs | The Athletic Stock Up WR Jalen Royals Second-year receiver Jalen Royals, after a slow start in training camp the last few weeks, had his best pro game. A 2025 fourth-round pick, Royals led the Chiefs with six catches for 51 yards while showing elusiveness in the open field. “It was great to see Royals step up and have a couple nice catches,” Chiefs coach Andy Reid said. “And then the yards after the catch, I thought, were nice. He did a nice job there.” 5 takeaways from Kansas City Chiefs’ preseason loss at Tampa Bay | KSHB 41 1. Do Chiefs have OT problem? A rookie minicamp invitee, Benson was a pleasant surprise, but the reality of NFL life may be setting in. He was flagged for a false start later allowed a strip sack when Anthony Nelson beat him around the edge to get to Fields. Moore also looked shaky in pass protection, albeit out of position, but that’s not a great place to be with a franchise QB returning from a major knee surgery. “We don’t have all the guys out there, but I like the chances of looking at the young guys and seeing what we’ve got there,” Reid said. “I’m OK with the O-line. We’ve got to keep working, but we’ll be all right there.” Patrick Mahomes says he’s ‘extremely confident’ he’ll play Week 1 vs. Broncos | FOX 4 While Mahomes has yet to see the field in the preseason following the torn ACL, he spoke about his return to play on the sideline with Trent Green in the Chiefs’ second preseason game vs. Tampa Bay. “I’m ready to be on that field,” Mahomes said. “I’ll try to play next week, but that’s up to coach (Andy) Reid.” Mahomes also stated that he tried to play in this week’s game, but that wasn’t his decision. He also stated that he’s “extremely confident” he’ll play against the defending AFC West champions in Week 1, barring any setbacks. Around the NFL Bills star DT Ed Oliver mourning tragic death of son | ESPN The 2-year-old son of Buffalo Bills defensive tackle Ed Oliver died June 28 after he was found unresponsive in a swimming pool by family members at a residence outside Houston. Oliver and his family have been mourning the tragic loss, and he is asking, according to a source close to him, for “privacy and prayers at this very difficult time.” The Bills acknowledged the tragedy in a statement Saturday. Browns’ Todd Monken not ready to name starting QB; Sanders scores, Watson peeved by boos | NFL.com Was it enough for the second-year QB to earn the starting gig? Browns coach Todd Monken had mostly positive things to say after the game about Sanders’ play and approach. “There’s a lot there to like,” Monken said. “He plays with a certain amount of confidence. He has gotten a lot better at getting rid of the ball. Certainly, he wants to make a play. “I thought he did a lot of good things. I’m really proud of him and where he’s come from the moment I got here until now. Very impressive.” Patriots rookie QB Behren Morton fills in at punter, then throws game-winning TD | Pro Football Talk Morton did his most important job by playing well when running the offense late in the game, throwing the game-winning 37-yard touchdown pass in the final minute. But Morton also showed he can be counted on in a pinch by punting very well after the Patriots’ regular punter, Bryce Baringer, left the game because he wasn’t feeling well. In Baringer’s absence, Morton punted three times for a 44.3-yard average. “Tonight was fun. I wasn’t expecting to punt. It’s been since high school since I’ve punted. You’ve just got to make the most of your opportunity when it comes, so I tried to do that tonight,” Morton said. In case you missed it on Arrowhead Pride 5 instant takeaways from Chiefs’ Preseason Week 2 3. Kahlil Benson doesn’t look ready for right tackle On two other plays, Benson poorly held up in pass protection; the second play led to a strip sack of quarterback Justin Fields, although Benson was aware enough to try and advance the fumble himself. The Chiefs needed to see Benson in live action on the right edge; Saturday was a great challenge, with Tampa Bay’s starting defense seeing extended playing time. It seemingly gave the answer Kansas City needed; Benson doesn’t look ready for the likes of Denver Broncos’ edge rusher Nik Bonitto in Week 1.
